03-Statistics/CRA Public Statistical Dat.body:
# CRA Public Statistical Data

The Canada Revenue Agency publishes **aggregate** statistical products derived from processed tax and benefit returns and related administrative data. These publications support public transparency and research; they do **not** contain taxpayer-identifiable records.

## Primary product family in this vault

- [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]] — formerly **T1 Final Statistics**; landing page lists editions by publication year and tax year (for example, 2026 edition for the 2024 tax year, 2025 edition for the 2023 tax year).
- Open Government Portal datasets mirror selected editions (see [[99-Sources/source-notes/SRC-CRA-T1-Stats-2023]]).

## Relationship to performance reporting

Operational highlights such as return volumes and digital filing rates appear in departmental planning and results documents (for example [[Electronic Filing Statistics]] sourced from the 2026–27 Departmental Plan **actual** 2024–25 “CRA by the numbers” section). Those figures are **not** the same series as T1 assessment-based tables and must be labelled by fiscal year and source.

## Limitations common to CRA public statistics

Published CRA aggregate tables are constrained by [[Public Data Confidentiality Procedures]], [[Data Suppression]], and [[Rounding]], and by [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]] choices that affect [[Initial Assessment Data]] versus [[Reassessment Data]]. When comparing editions, apply [[Comparability Across Editions]] and expect [[Statistical Revision]].

## Audit and analytics relevance

Analytical work that joins CRA public statistics to audit populations should document these limitations and their effect on [[Small-Cell Analysis]] and [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]].

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (landing)](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics.html)
- [[99-Sources/CRA-Public-Source-Register]]

03-Statistics/Comparability Across Editi.title: Comparability Across Editions
03-Statistics/Comparability Across Editi.body:
# Comparability Across Editions

**Individual Income Tax Return Statistics** are published as **editions** (publication year) tied to a **tax year**. Trend analysis requires aligning tax year, cut-off date, classifications, and table geography rules.

## Extraction time frame changes

Starting with the **2025 edition (2023 tax year)**, CRA adopted an **earlier extraction cut-off** (**November 30, 2024** versus **June 30, 2025** referenced for the prior approach) to improve **timeliness**. Official guidance: when comparing this edition with **previous editions**, **differences in extraction time frames** should be taken into consideration.

Effects include:

- Lower counts or amounts versus a later cut-off for the **same tax year** when reassessments and late processing continue after November 30.
- Breaks in time series if earlier editions used a longer post-tax-year processing window.

## Other comparability factors

| Factor | Consideration |
|--------|----------------|
| Tax year vs edition year | Landing page lists edition year and tax year (for example 2026 edition for 2024 tax year) |
| Geography | Taxation (Table 1) vs residence (Tables 2–5) — [[Tax Statistics by Area]] |
| Income grouping | Range boundaries and line item definitions — [[Tax Statistics by Tax Bracket]] |
| Disclosure | [[Data Suppression]] and [[Rounding]] rules may be stable but still distort level changes in small cells |
| Revision | [[Statistical Revision]] may update an edition |

## Distinction from departmental operational metrics

Fiscal-year **actual** highlights (for example [[Electronic Filing Statistics]] for **2024–25**) are not directly comparable to tax-year assessment tables without explicit mapping.

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year)](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics/2023-tax-year.html)
- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (landing)](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics.html)
- [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]]

03-Statistics/Data Suppression.md.title: Data Suppression
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
03-Statistics/Data Suppression.md.body:
# Data Suppression

In CRA **Individual Income Tax Return Statistics**, **data are suppressed where warranted** to protect tax filer information under [[Public Data Confidentiality Procedures]].

## How suppression appears in tables

- A **zero [0]** in a cell means the value is **suppressed for confidentiality**, not necessarily a true zero count or amount.
- Suppressed information **includes valid zeroes** (a filer count or dollar amount that is genuinely zero may still be withheld when disclosure rules require).
- **Totals may not equal** the sum of displayed detail because of suppression (and [[Rounding]]).

## Implications for analysis

Suppression creates **structural missingness** in public tables. Analysts cannot recover suppressed cells from published CSV/PDF outputs. Joins to audit samples by fine-grained dimensions (small provinces, rare income ranges, intersection of age and source of income) often align with suppressed cells—see [[Small-Cell Analysis]].

For a general profession-wide treatment of suppression and disclosure control, see also references in [[06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Analytics]] when a dedicated concept note is added under `06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/`.

## Linkage in the vault

[[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]] → constrained by [[Data Suppression]] (with [[Rounding]], [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]], [[Comparability Across Editions]]) → affects [[Small-Cell Analysis]] → relevant to [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]].

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year) — Confidentiality procedures](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics/2023-tax-year.html)
- [[Public Data Confidentiality Procedures]]

03-Statistics/Individual Income Tax Retu.title: Individual Income Tax Return Statistics
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
03-Statistics/Individual Income Tax Retu.body:
# Individual Income Tax Return Statistics

**Individual Income Tax Return Statistics** presents data from individual income tax and benefit returns processed for a stated **tax year**. The series was formerly known as **T1 Final Statistics**. Each **edition** (publication year) corresponds to a tax year and includes explanatory notes, PDF/CSV tables, and (for recent editions) an Open Government dataset.

## 2025 edition — 2023 tax year (verified 2026-07-23)

Authoritative scope for the edition documented in this vault:

- Data are from returns **processed for the 2023 tax year**.
- Statistics include the most recent **2023 tax year assessments or reassessments** up to the cut-off date **November 30, 2024**.
- Starting with this edition, CRA uses an **earlier extraction cut-off** (November 30, 2024 versus June 30, 2025 in prior practice) to increase timeliness; when comparing editions, **extraction time frames** must be taken into account ([[Comparability Across Editions]], [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]]).
- The **most recent assessment** is used; for reassessed returns, the **most current reassessed values** are used ([[Reassessment Data]]).
- **All statistics in the publication are subject to revision** ([[Statistical Revision]]).

Landing page for all editions: [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (formerly T1 Final Statistics)](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics.html) (lists editions through **2026** for the **2024 tax year**).

Open data: [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year)](https://open.canada.ca/data/en/dataset/5954b30b-9179-4f4c-adca-445372df4c60).

## Table structure (2023 tax year edition)

| Table | Geography / dimension | Notes |
|-------|------------------------|-------|
| **Table 1** | Province or territory of **taxation** | Only table using **taxation** jurisdiction (not residence); includes **outside Canada** ([[Tax Statistics by Area]]) |
| **Table 2** | Income ranges; provincial/territorial residence where split | Line items by [[Tax Statistics by Tax Bracket]] (income ranges on total income assessed) |
| **Table 3** | Source of income by province/territory of **residence** | Nine source-of-income groups |
| **Table 4** | Age and gender | Residence-based provincial tables |
| **Table 5** | Province or territory of **residence** | Line items by jurisdiction of residence |

Tables 2, 4, and 5 present statistics for tax line items grouped under income ranges, age, gender, and province or territory of residence, as described on the official page. Dollar amounts and counts in tables are subject to [[Public Data Confidentiality Procedures]], [[Data Suppression]], and [[Rounding]]; totals may not add due to suppression or rounding.

## Statistical limitations chain

[[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]] → constrained by [[Data Suppression]], [[Rounding]], [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]], [[Comparability Across Editions]] → affects [[Small-Cell Analysis]] → relevant to [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]].

## Related notes

- [[CRA Public Statistical Data]]
- [[Initial Assessment Data]]
- [[Reassessment Data]]

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year)](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics/2023-tax-year.html)
- [[99-Sources/source-notes/SRC-CRA-T1-Stats-2023]]

03-Statistics/Initial Assessment Data.md.title: Initial Assessment Data
03-Statistics/Initial Assessment Data.md.body:
# Initial Assessment Data

In **Individual Income Tax Return Statistics**, each return contributes the values from its **most recent assessment** available as of the [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]]. For returns never reassessed by that date, the published figures reflect the **initial assessment** (first assessment recorded in the extraction window).

## Official compilation rule

CRA states that the **most recent assessment** is used to compile the statistics. Returns **not yet reassessed** by the cut-off therefore appear with **initial assessment** line values.

## Contrast with reassessed returns

When CRA completes a **reassessment** on or before the cut-off, tables use **reassessed values** instead of the original assessment ([[Reassessment Data]]). The publication does not separately flag which cells are initial versus reassessed at the aggregate level.

## Revision over time

Later editions or [[Statistical Revision]] can replace initial-assessment-based figures when reassessments post-date an earlier cut-off.

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year) — Explanatory notes](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics/2023-tax-year.html)
- [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]]

03-Statistics/Public Data Confidentialit.title: Public Data Confidentiality Procedures
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
03-Statistics/Public Data Confidentialit.body:
# Public Data Confidentiality Procedures

For **Individual Income Tax Return Statistics**, CRA applies confidentiality procedures **to ensure the protection of tax filer information**.

## Published rules (2023 tax year edition)

Official explanatory notes state:

- Data have been **suppressed where warranted** (see [[Data Suppression]]).
- **Counts** are rounded to the nearest multiple of **10** ([[Rounding]]).
- **Dollar amounts** in Tables 1 to 5 are rounded to the nearest **thousand**.
- **Totals may not add** due to rounding or suppression.
- A displayed **zero [0]** indicates information **suppressed for confidentiality**; suppressed cells can include **valid zeroes**.

Table footnotes direct readers to these procedures when row or column totals do not match summed cells.

## Relationship to general concepts

Profession-wide disclosure-control concepts are available in [[Data Suppression — Audit Application]]. This note records **CRA’s published implementation** for the T1 aggregate statistics product.

## Audit relevance

When public CRA tables are used as [[Evidence]], auditors should treat suppressed or rounded cells as limiting precision for [[Small-Cell Analysis]] and for [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]].

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year) — Confidentiality procedures](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics/2023-tax-year.html)
- [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]]

03-Statistics/Reassessment Data.md.title: Reassessment Data
03-Statistics/Reassessment Data.md.body:
# Reassessment Data

**Individual Income Tax Return Statistics** incorporate **reassessments** completed on or before the [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]] for the stated tax year.

## Official rule

For returns that have been **reassessed**, CRA uses the **most current reassessed values** to prepare the tables. The **most recent assessment** (whether initial or reassessed) drives published aggregates.

## Coverage window

Statistics contain the most recent assessments or reassessments for the tax year **up to the edition’s cut-off date** (for the 2023 tax year 2025 edition: **November 30, 2024**). Reassessments finalized **after** that date are excluded until a subsequent edition or [[Statistical Revision]].

## Analytical caution

Aggregate tables mix initial and reassessed outcomes without filer-level flags. Comparisons to audit **reassessment yield** or collections timelines (see evaluation themes in [[99-Sources/source-notes/SRC-CRA-Eval-Audit-Yield-2020]]) require different data sources and periods.

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year) — Explanatory notes](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics/2023-tax-year.html)
- [[Initial Assessment Data]]
- [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]]

03-Statistics/Rounding.md.title: Rounding
03-Statistics/Rounding.md.body:
# Rounding

CRA applies explicit **rounding rules** in **Individual Income Tax Return Statistics** as part of [[Public Data Confidentiality Procedures]].

## Rules (2023 tax year edition)

Official explanatory notes specify:

| Measure | Rounding rule |
|---------|----------------|
| **Counts** | Nearest multiple of **10** (example: 104 → 100; 105 → 110) |
| **Dollar amounts** (Tables 1–5) | Nearest **thousand** |

**Totals may not add** due to rounding or [[Data Suppression]].

## Audit and analytics implications

- Reconciliation of published totals to micro-level calculations will show **immaterial differences** even without suppression.
- Rate calculations (for example dollars per return) inherit rounding error; small denominators amplify apparent variance ([[Small-Cell Analysis]]).
- Rounding is distinct from [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]] effects but combines with them when comparing editions ([[Comparability Across Editions]]).

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year) — Confidentiality procedures](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics/2023-tax-year.html)
- [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]]

03-Statistics/Statistical Revision.md.title: Statistical Revision
03-Statistics/Statistical Revision.md.body:
# Statistical Revision

CRA states that **all statistics** in **Individual Income Tax Return Statistics** are **subject to revision**.

## Drivers of revision

Revisions can arise when:

- Additional returns are **processed** after an edition’s [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]].
- **Reassessments** update line values ([[Reassessment Data]]).
- CRA republishes an edition or releases a new edition for the same tax year with an extended cut-off ([[Comparability Across Editions]]).
- Methodological or classification updates are documented in explanatory notes (for example new tax credits or line items for a tax year).

Open Government dataset metadata may show a **resource update date** distinct from the tax year; users should cite the edition URL and access date.

## Audit documentation

When citing a published CRA table in workpapers, record **edition year**, **tax year**, **cut-off date**, and **access date** so revision is traceable.

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year) — Explanatory notes](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics/2023-tax-year.html)
- [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]]

03-Statistics/Tax Statistics by Area.md.title: Tax Statistics by Area
03-Statistics/Tax Statistics by Area.md.body:
# Tax Statistics by Area

In [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]], geographic breakdowns use two different concepts. Mixing them without relabelling invalidates comparisons.

## Province or territory of taxation (Table 1)

**Table 1 – General statement by province and territory of taxation** is the **only** table in the 2023 tax year edition that uses **province or territory of taxation** rather than residence.

Official definition: province or territory of taxation is the jurisdiction in which **provincial or territorial tax is payable**.

Table 1 presents key statistics by taxation jurisdiction for all returns (non-taxable and taxable) and includes returns from **outside Canada**.

## Province or territory of residence (Tables 2–5)

For **Tables 2, 4, and 5**, provincial and territorial subtables use **province or territory of residence**: the jurisdiction where the tax filer **resided on December 31** of the tax year, as reported on the return.

**Table 3** shows returns by **source of income** and province or territory of **residence**.

**Table 5** classifies returns according to residence listed on the return.

## Audit and analytics caution

Joining external datasets to CRA area statistics requires matching the same geography field (taxation vs residence). Small populations in a province or territory may trigger [[Data Suppression]] and affect [[Small-Cell Analysis]].

## Sources

- [Individual Income Tax Return Statistics (2023 tax year) — Provincial or territorial classification; Description of tables](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/income-statistics-gst-hst-statistics/t1-final-statistics/2023-tax-year.html)
- [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]]

03-Statistics/Tax Statistics by Tax Brac.title: Tax Statistics by Tax Bracket
03-Statistics/Tax Statistics by Tax Brac.body:
# Tax Statistics by Tax Bracket

In CRA’s **Individual Income Tax Return Statistics**, distributional tables group filers by **income ranges** based on **total income assessed** (T1 line 15000), not by statutory **marginal tax rate brackets**. This note uses the vault title “tax bracket” as a colloquial entry point; the official classification is **income ranges**.

## Table 2 — Tax return line items by income ranges

**Table 2** presents tax return line items cross-tabulated by income ranges. The table begins with total returns, then ranges from **$4,999 and under** through **$250,000 and over**. National and provincial/territorial tables use **province or territory of residence** ([[Tax Statistics by Area]]).

Income ranges are based on **total income assessed**, which includes employment, pension, investment, self-employment, other sources, and non-taxable income components as defined in the publication. Total income assessed may differ from economic income in other publications because certain non-taxable amounts are excluded while some grossed-up amounts (for example eligible dividends) may be included.

## Taxable vs non-taxable (related classification)

The publication also classifies returns as **taxable** or **non-taxable** using a rule based on the sum of net federal tax, net provincial tax, CPP/EI on self-employment, and social benefit repayments (taxable if that sum is at least **$2**). High total-income filers may still be non-taxable after deductions and credits.

## Limitations

Range-level counts and dollars are rounded and may be suppressed ([[Rounding]], [[Data Suppression]]). Sparse ranges exacerbate [[Small-Cell Analysis]] issues when linking to audit samples.

04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Client.md.title: Audit Client
04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Client.md.body:
**Content class:** general professional / teaching term **audit client** (or auditee). **Official case-specific** labels in CRA public reports often use **OPI**, management response owner, or **MAP owner** instead of the phrase “audit client.”

The **audit client** is the management party responsible for the subject under review: it provides access and [[Evidence]], clarifies process facts, receives [[Finding]]s, and submits [[Management Response]] / [[Management Action Plan]] commitments. The client **cooperates** with internal audit; it is **not** the auditor and does not perform independent assurance ([[Internal Audit Independence]]).

In CRA vault usage, **Office of Primary Interest (OPI)** means the business area primarily responsible for the audited subject ([[CRA-Acronym-Dictionary]]). OPI aligns with audit-client responsibility for scope and accountability but may not name every interviewed or co-responsible partner. [[Scope]] defines what is in the engagement; OPI identifies who management designates as primary accountable party for that scope in report language.

Other branches (e.g., [[Information Technology Branch|ITB]] as technical support) may be in scope, interviewed, or named in action plans without being OPI/MAP lead— see [[Ownership and Assurance Roles]] BI and EFMS examples.

04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Conclusion.md.title: Audit Conclusion
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Conclusion.md.body:
An **audit conclusion** is the engagement-level statement of what was determined relative to the [[Audit Objective]], [[Scope]], and [[Criteria]]. It differs from individual [[Finding]]s and from [[Recommendation]]s.

Conclusion **strength** must match evidence strength ([[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]], [[Evidence Reliability]]). When [[Population Completeness]] cannot be established, narrow wording to the [[Retrieved Population]], qualify, or use directional language—do not imply coverage of the full [[Intended Population]].

[[Reasonable Assurance]] is high but not absolute; sampling, data, and system limits remain.

04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Logging.md.title: Audit Logging
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Logging.md.body:
**Audit logging** records security- or control-relevant events (access, changes, privileged activity, control-relevant alerts) into an **audit trail**. Distinct from [[Application Logging]] (business/transaction events) and from [[Security Logging]] when the latter is used only for tool telemetry—though they overlap in practice.

Logs can be strong [[System-Generated Evidence]] only when protected from tampering, retained appropriately ([[Data Retention]]), complete enough for the assertion, time-consistent ([[Time Synchronization]]), and attributable ([[Identity Attribution]]). Gaps, weak access to logs, or unknown retention reduce [[Evidence Reliability]]. **Do not** treat system-generated logs as complete without validation ([[Incomplete Audit Logging]], [[Population Completeness]]).

**Generation ≠ review:** configuring logging is not the same control as [[Log Review]] or [[Monitoring and Alerting]]. Related broader concept: [[Monitoring and Reporting]].

04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Objective.md.title: Audit Objective
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Objective.md.body:
The **audit objective** states what the audit is intended to accomplish: the subject matter being examined and the purpose of the examination. It answers why the audit is being performed and what assurance or insight stakeholders should gain. A clear objective anchors planning, scope, criteria, and reporting so that work remains focused and conclusions remain traceable to the stated intent.

Objectives are typically expressed in terms of evaluating whether controls, processes, or outcomes meet defined criteria within a specified scope. They may seek reasonable assurance that risks are managed appropriately, that compliance requirements are met, or that resources are used efficiently and effectively. Precision matters: vague objectives invite scope creep and make it difficult to judge whether the audit succeeded.

In internal audit, objectives align with the organization's risk profile and the internal audit function's charter. They should be agreed or communicated to management and, where relevant, those charged with governance before fieldwork begins. When objectives change materially during the engagement, the change should be documented and understood by stakeholders.

Objectives differ from scope (what is included and excluded) and from criteria (the benchmarks used to evaluate the subject matter). Together, objective, scope, and criteria form the engagement specification that drives methodology and evidence requirements.

04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Observation.md.title: Audit Observation
04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Observation.md.body:
An **audit observation** is a noted condition from fieldwork that has **not** (yet) been elevated to a formal [[Finding]]. Immaterial exceptions or isolated errors may remain observations communicated to management without public-report treatment ([[Finding]]).

**Disambiguation:** this note is **not** the testing procedure of watching a process. For the procedure, see [[Observation (Procedure)]].

```text
Evidence → Audit Observation → (assessed against Criteria) → may become Finding
```

State the audit period when interpreting [[Finding]]s. Historical public findings describe conditions in that period—not automatically current conditions. See [[Interpreting Historical Public Audit Findings]].

outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
04-Audit-Concepts/Audit Planning.md.body:
**Audit planning** is the work that turns an assurance need into an executable engagement: clarify the [[Audit Objective]], draft [[Scope]] (including exclusions and [[Audit Period]]), select [[Criteria]], assess [[Risk Assessment|engagement risk]], and design [[Methodology]] / [[Control Testing]] procedures so that [[Evidence]] will be sufficient and appropriate.

Planning is iterative. [[Risk Assessment]] and preliminary inquiries may refine scope before fieldwork. Material changes should be documented and communicated to the [[Audit Client]].

**Content class:** general professional knowledge. Individual CRA reports may describe planning approvals (e.g., Assignment Planning Memorandum) as **official case-specific** facts when stated.

04-Audit-Concepts/Automated Control.md.title: Automated Control
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
04-Audit-Concepts/Automated Control.md.body:
An **automated control** is performed by a system (validations, detection rules, automated workflows)—often expressed as [[Automated Business Rules]].

**Design** tests examine whether logic/configuration is capable of meeting the [[Control Objective]] ([[Design Effectiveness]]). **Implementation** asks whether the approved rule was actually deployed/configured ([[Control Implementation]], [[System Configuration]], [[Deployment Approval]]). **Operating effectiveness** asks whether the rule remained enabled and operated over the [[Audit Period]]—including mid-period changes ([[Change Management]], [[Operating Effectiveness]]).

**Bypass path:** [[Manual Overrides]] can defeat an otherwise effective automated control if approval, logging, and [[Exception Report Review]] are weak. Overrides may be legitimate; test the governance path, not only the happy path.

**Reliance rules:** ITGCs—access and change management—usually required ([[IT Controls]], [[Tool Deployment]], [[System-Generated Evidence]]). Source-code or config inspection alone does not prove period OE. Pre-production testing does not prove production OE for the whole period. Assess outcomes via [[False Positives]] / [[False Negatives]] where relevant.

04-Audit-Concepts/Consequence or Impact..body:

Consequence is not the same as root cause ([[Root Cause Analysis]]) and not the same as the recommendation.

04-Audit-Concepts/Control Deficiency.md.body:

Weak or missing controls increase exposure and **may** support a [[Finding]] when paired with [[Evidence]] of adverse conditions—but **not every** deficiency is reportable ([[Risk]], [[Finding]]).

04-Audit-Concepts/Control Frequency.md.body:

04-Audit-Concepts/Control Implementation.title: Control Implementation
04-Audit-Concepts/Control Implementation.body:
**Control implementation** is whether the designed [[Control]] has been put in place (procedure issued, rule deployed, reviewer assigned, tool configured). Implementation sits between [[Design Effectiveness]] and [[Operating Effectiveness]]: a well-designed control that was never implemented cannot operate; an implemented control may still fail OE testing.

For automated rules: approved requirement → build/[[Code Review]] → [[Deployment Approval]] → production [[System Configuration]]. **Pre-production test evidence (UAT/SIT) supports implementation readiness but does not demonstrate [[Operating Effectiveness]] in production throughout the [[Audit Period]].**

04-Audit-Concepts/Control Testing.md.body:
**Control testing** is the set of procedures used to evaluate [[Design Effectiveness]], [[Control Implementation]], and [[Operating Effectiveness]]. Common procedures: [[Document Review]], [[Walkthrough]], [[Inquiry]], [[Observation (Procedure)]], [[Inspection]], [[Configuration Review]], [[Reperformance]], [[Exception Testing]], [[Sample Selection]], data analysis ([[Analytics]] / [[Full-Population Analysis]]).

Select procedures based on control type ([[Manual Control]] vs [[Automated Control]]), frequency, risk, and available evidence. Always link tests to [[Control Objective]], [[Criteria]], and required [[Evidence]]. For access controls see [[Access Review Testing]]; for pipelines see [[Data Reconciliation]] and source-to-report tracing.

04-Audit-Concepts/Control.md.title: Control
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory
Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
04-Audit-Concepts/Control.md.body:
A **control** is a policy, procedure, practice, or mechanism designed to provide reasonable assurance that objectives will be achieved and risks mitigated. Controls may be preventive (stop errors or fraud before they occur), detective (identify issues after they occur), or corrective (remediate and improve). They operate at entity, process, and transaction levels.

Auditors evaluate [[Design Effectiveness]] (whether the control, if operated as intended, would address the [[Control Objective]] / [[Risk]]) and [[Operating Effectiveness]] (whether it actually functioned over the [[Audit Period]] at the required [[Control Frequency]], by the right person/system, with sufficient evidence). See [[Control Testing]].

Control testing may use [[Walkthrough]], [[Inquiry]], [[Observation (Procedure)]], [[Inspection]], [[Reperformance]], or [[Analytics]]. **[[Inquiry]] alone does not demonstrate operating effectiveness** for the period—corroborate with other [[Evidence]]. A walkthrough is primarily a design/understanding tool, not full-period OE testing. Documentation that a control exists is not proof it operated ([[Control Ownership]]).

Weak or missing controls are a [[Control Deficiency]]; they increase [[Risk]] and may support [[Finding]]s when paired with evidence of adverse conditions—but not every deficiency is reportable.

Control frameworks (e.g., COSO internal control components, COBIT for IT) help structure reviews. [[IT Controls]] and [[Security Controls]] are specialized subsets. Clear [[Control Ownership]] supports accountability for design, operation, and remediation.

Controls are not guarantees; they reduce risk to an acceptable level within cost and operational constraints. Over-reliance on manual controls, compensating controls, or undocumented practices are common review themes in professional audit literature.

04-Audit-Concepts/Criteria.md.title: Criteria
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory
Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
04-Audit-Concepts/Criteria.md.body:
**Criteria** are the benchmarks or standards against which audit subject matter is evaluated. They may be laws, regulations, policies, professional standards, control frameworks, service-level agreements, budgets, or internally adopted performance targets. Without agreed criteria, auditors cannot consistently determine whether conditions represent deficiencies, exceptions, or acceptable variation.

Criteria should be suitable, available, and clearly linked to the audit objective and scope. Suitable criteria are relevant, reliable, and understandable to intended users. When multiple criteria apply (e.g., legal minimum versus best practice), the audit report should clarify which were used and how conflicts were resolved.

In internal audit, criteria often include organizational policies, risk appetite statements, and control design expectations. External assurance engagements may reference COSO, COBIT, ISO standards, or sector-specific requirements. Auditors document how criteria were selected and whether management agreed to them.

Findings typically describe a condition, compare it to criteria, identify cause where practicable, and assess effect or risk. Weak or unstated criteria undermine the defensibility of [[Finding]]s and [[Recommendation]]s.

04-Audit-Concepts/Design Effectiveness.m.body:

Typical design work: understand the risk; inspect policies/configs; [[Walkthrough]]; assess logic of automated rules ([[Automated Control]], [[IT Controls]]). A walkthrough that confirms understanding of design is **not** by itself [[Operating Effectiveness]] testing for the whole [[Audit Period]].

Documentation of a control’s design is not proof it operated.

04-Audit-Concepts/Evidence Evaluation.md.title: Evidence Evaluation
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
04-Audit-Concepts/Evidence Evaluation.md.body:
**Evidence evaluation** is the analysis step between collecting [[Evidence]] and drafting a [[Finding]]:

```text
Evidence → analyze → observed condition → compare to Criteria → Finding (if significant for reporting)
```

Here **“significant” means audit-report significance** (worthy of elevation given [[Materiality]] / [[Operational Significance]])—**not** [[Statistical Significance]] from a hypothesis test.

Evaluate sufficiency (quantity/coverage), appropriateness (relevance + reliability), corroboration, and limitations. Match conclusion strength to evidence strength ([[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]]). Use [[Professional Judgment]]; do not conclude before considering evidence. Lack of statistical significance does not prove absence of risk ([[Rare High-Impact Events]]).

04-Audit-Concepts/Evidence Hierarchy.md.title: Evidence Hierarchy
04-Audit-Concepts/Evidence Hierarchy.md.body:
**Evidence hierarchy** (teaching scale—not an official CRA rule) compares typical persuasiveness of evidence forms. More items from one weak source do not fix a reliability problem ([[Evidence Reliability]]).

| Form | Typical use | Caveat |
|---|---|---|
| [[Inquiry]] | Understanding | Not standalone OE proof |
| Documents / procedures | Design / intent | May not prove operation |
| System reports / dashboards | Analytics / monitoring | Need lineage, config, definitions |
| [[Audit Logging|Logs]] / trails | Automated detective controls | Must be protected and complete |
| [[Observation (Procedure)]] | Point-in-time | Not full-period OE alone |
| [[Inspection]] of period evidence | OE sampling | Frame/population errors |
| [[Reperformance]] / independent [[Analytics]] | Strong OE | Depends on complete source data |

Always corroborate management representations ([[Evidence]]). No universal numeric threshold for sufficiency ([[Missing Data]]).

04-Audit-Concepts/Evidence.md.title: Evidence
outgoing_links: How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance
Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory
04-Audit-Concepts/Evidence.md.body:
**Evidence** (audit evidence) comprises the information used by auditors to support findings, conclusions, and opinions. It should be sufficient, appropriate, and reliable for the purpose of the engagement. **Sufficiency** relates to quantity and coverage; **appropriateness** relates to relevance and reliability/persuasiveness ([[Evidence Reliability]]). Evidence is assessed **against [[Criteria]] within [[Scope]]** for the [[Audit Objective]]. Together these determine whether an informed third party could reach the same conclusions from the same facts.

More low-quality items from one weak source do **not** resolve a reliability problem. There is **no** universal numeric evidence threshold ([[Missing Data]]). Prefer corroboration and, where needed, alternative evidence. See [[Evidence Hierarchy]] and [[System-Generated Evidence]].

Evidence types include documents, data extracts, system configurations, interview notes, observations, external confirmations, and analytical procedures. Digital evidence raises questions of integrity, completeness, and chain of custody. Auditors document how evidence was obtained, who provided it, and any limitations (e.g., partial populations, redactions, or system cut-off dates)—forms of [[Missing Data]] that reduce sufficiency even when remaining items are accurate.

Professional standards emphasize skepticism: corroborating management representations, validating source systems, and understanding context before accepting data at face value. Related concepts in data-intensive audits include [[Evidence Reliability]], [[Data Quality]], and [[Structured Data]] versus [[Unstructured Information]].

Working papers retain evidence linkages so that [[Finding]]s can be traced to tested [[Control]]s and [[Criteria]]. When evidence is incomplete, auditors may scope-limit conclusions or qualify reporting.

04-Audit-Concepts/Finding.md.body:
An audit **finding** communicates a significant issue identified during the engagement. Explanatory structure (reports may not use these exact headings):

```text
[[Evidence]] → condition
→ compare to [[Criteria]]
→ [[Root Cause Analysis|cause]] (when supported—do not invent)
→ [[Consequence or Impact|consequence / risk]]
→ [[Recommendation]]
```

Common elements: **condition** (what was observed), **criteria** (expected state), **cause** (why, when known), and **effect** / [[Consequence or Impact]] (actual or potential impact). Some frameworks add recommendation within the finding; this vault often separates [[Recommendation]].

Workflow: [[Evidence Evaluation]] → [[Audit Observation]] → (may become) Finding. Not every observation or [[Control Deficiency]] becomes a formal finding—immaterial exceptions may be noted to management without public report treatment ([[Materiality]], [[Operational Significance]]). Aggregation matters. Report “significance” is not the same as [[Statistical Significance]].

Findings should be fact-based, supported by [[Evidence]], and discussed with management when practicable. They differ from recommendations (proposed remedies) and from conclusions (overall engagement judgments). Historical public findings are period-bound—[[Interpreting Historical Public Audit Findings]].

**Inquiry discipline:** a risk indicator or line of inquiry is not a finding. Path before elevation: risk indicator → inquiry → evidence request → procedure → analysis → possible observation—only then condition vs [[Criteria]] ([[Cross-Domain Audit Map]], [[Grounded-Audit-Inquiry-Guidelines]], [[Professional Judgment]]).

In public sector reporting, findings may relate to compliance, value for money, governance, or program results. Case studies in this vault may link specific published reports to these general elements without inventing organization-specific content in concept notes.

04-Audit-Concepts/Follow-up.md.title: Follow-up
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
04-Audit-Concepts/Follow-up.md.body:
**Follow-up** (or follow-up auditing) verifies whether management implemented agreed actions from prior audits and whether those actions effectively addressed [[Finding]]s and residual [[Risk]]. Implementation status is not assumed from MAP target dates alone, and verifying implementation does **not** automatically prove ongoing operating effectiveness without testing. Follow-up closes the loop between reporting and sustained improvement and holds parties accountable for commitments in [[Management Response]] and [[Management Action Plan]] items—without transferring ownership of controls to Internal Audit ([[Internal Audit Independence]]).

Follow-up procedures may include status interviews, document inspection, data re-testing, and walkthroughs of updated [[Control]]s. Outcomes are often reported as implemented, partially implemented, not implemented, or no longer applicable (with justification). Persistent gaps may be re-reported or escalated to governance.

Timing depends on risk, complexity, and agreed due dates. High-risk items may be tracked continuously; lower-risk items may be bundled in periodic follow-up reports. Internal audit functions typically maintain a recommendation tracking register.

Follow-up is distinct from a new audit: it focuses on prior commitments rather than a fresh risk assessment of the entire area—though persistent failure may trigger a broader re-audit.

04-Audit-Concepts/Full-Population Analys.title: Full-Population Analysis
04-Audit-Concepts/Full-Population Analys.body:
**Full-population analysis** tests all records in the available [[Retrieved Population]] with [[Analytics]] when data allow. It **reduces** [[Sampling Risk]] (sampling variability) but does **not** eliminate audit risk.

**Benefits:** broader coverage of the available set; detection of rare/concentrated exceptions; segmentation/comparisons; patterns across the extract.

**Residual risks:** incomplete [[Intended Population]]; extraction/transform errors ([[Data Pipeline]], [[Data Lineage]]); duplicates ([[Record Uniqueness]]); inaccurate fields ([[Data Accuracy]]); changing definitions ([[Comparability Across Editions]]); poor rule/query logic; [[False Positives]]; inappropriate interpretation ([[Analytical Validity]], [[Operational Significance]]). In very large datasets, tiny effects may be statistically detectable yet immaterial ([[Statistical Significance]], [[Effect Size]], [[Materiality]]).

Require [[Reproducibility]] of code/parameters/sources—and separately judge [[Analytical Validity]]. State when conclusions apply only to the retrieved subset.

04-Audit-Concepts/Internal Audit Indepen.title: Internal Audit Independence
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Specific Cyber Security Controls
04-Audit-Concepts/Internal Audit Indepen.body:
**Content class:** general professional concept for independence; **official public CRA fact** that [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]] provides independent assurance and evaluation (branch mandate); **case-specific** where a report applies [[Three Lines Model]] language (e.g., cyber case third line).

**Internal audit independence** means the assurance function can perform work and report without undue influence from the activities it reviews. Independence supports objective [[Finding]]s, candid [[Recommendation]]s, and credible follow-up— it does **not** transfer ownership of business processes, systems, data, or corrective action to auditors.

At CRA, AERB publishes via [[Internal Audit and Program Evaluation]]; that publishing role is not the same as being MAP owner. Auditors may review draft [[Management Action Plan]]s for completeness but **do not own execution** ([[Management Action Plan]]). Management owns [[Management Response]] and remediation ([[Management Action Plan Owner]]).

The [[Three Lines Model]] places internal audit in the **third line**: assurance distinct from first-line control operation and second-line monitoring/challenge. TBS internal audit policy expectations for CAE independence and formal management responses appear in [[99-Sources/source-notes/SRC-TBS-Policy-Internal-Audit]].

Independence is preserved when auditors name reasonable MAPs— judging plans is assurance; implementing them remains management accountability.

04-Audit-Concepts/Internal Audit and Pro.title: Internal Audit and Program Evaluation
04-Audit-Concepts/Internal Audit and Pro.body:
**Internal audit and program evaluation** functions provide independent assurance and insight on governance, risk management, controls, and program performance. Internal audit typically follows professional standards (e.g., IIA Global Internal Audit Standards), emphasizes objectivity and a systematic methodology, and reports to audit committees or equivalent governance bodies. Program evaluation focuses on relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, and sometimes equity of programs, often using mixed methods and logic models.

Both disciplines share themes: clear [[Audit Objective]] and [[Scope]], defensible [[Evidence]], transparent [[Finding]]s, and actionable [[Recommendation]]s. Evaluation may place greater weight on outcomes measurement, counterfactual reasoning, and stakeholder perspectives; internal audit may emphasize control design and compliance with [[Criteria]]. In practice, functions may coexist in one shop or collaborate on integrated reviews.

Federal departments and agencies in Canada commonly publish selected internal audit and evaluation reports for transparency. The Canada Revenue Agency, like other organizations, may publish such reports on its public website; this vault may link official landing pages and case studies when source notes exist—see [[SRC-CRA-IA-PE-Landing]] when created in the organization or sources folders.

Concept notes here remain general; they do not assert specific CRA engagement outcomes.

04-Audit-Concepts/Interpreting Historica.body:
# Interpreting Historical Public Audit Findings

> **Derived onboarding note** — not a CRA policy.

When reading a public case:

1. Note **report date** and **[[Audit Period]]** (and examination dates if stated).
2. Treat published findings as evidence about **that period**.
3. Do **not** assume the same weakness remains today without a newer official source.
4. Treat [[Management Action Plan]] target dates as **commitments**, not proof of completion.
5. If the vault has **no follow-up evidence**, mark current remediation status **unknown**.
6. Separate **what the published report states** from **derived analysis** sections.
7. Never reconstruct protected/redacted content.

See [[08-Cases/README]] and case “Follow-up evidence in vault” sections.

04-Audit-Concepts/Management Action Plan.title: Management Action Plan Owner
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
04-Audit-Concepts/Management Action Plan.body:
**Content class:** general professional concept. **Official case-specific** when a published report names the branch or official agreeing to the [[Management Action Plan]] (MAP).

The **MAP owner** is management accountable for delivering the actions, milestones, and dates committed after audit [[Recommendation]]s— typically the same party as primary [[Audit Client]] / OPI for the engagement, but co-owners or named collaborators may appear for technical work. Ownership includes tracking progress, resourcing remediation, and updating [[Management Response]] when plans change.

MAP owners align actions with [[Control Ownership]] and root causes of [[Finding]]s. They do **not** include [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]] as executor: auditors assure and follow up; management implements ([[Internal Audit Independence]]).

**Examples (report-named only):**

- BI audit — [[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch|SIIB]] agrees; ITB and others named in collaboration ([[Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence]])
- EFMS audit — [[02-Organization/Branches/Security Branch]] MAP owner; [[Information Technology Branch|ITB]] jointly named for selected items ([[Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System]])

Other cases in the vault (ARNI, cyber, charities) use the same pattern: read each case org section for the named MAP owner rather than assuming a single enterprise rule.

04-Audit-Concepts/Management Action Plan.title: Management Action Plan
04-Audit-Concepts/Management Action Plan.body:
A **management action plan** (MAP) details how management will implement responses to audit [[Recommendation]]s. It typically lists actions, owners, resources, milestones, and target completion dates. MAPs translate [[Management Response]] commitments into trackable work suitable for project management and [[Follow-up]] verification.

Strong action plans align with [[Control Ownership]], address underlying causes of [[Finding]]s, and define how success will be measured (KPIs, control tests, or reduced exception rates). For IT-related issues, plans may reference [[Tool Deployment]], configuration changes, or [[Monitoring and Reporting]] enhancements.

Auditors may review draft MAPs for completeness but do not own execution. Governance bodies sometimes monitor overdue MAP items. When dates slip, management should document revised timelines and risk acceptance decisions.

In multi-year remediation, plans may phase quick wins and structural changes. Linkage to [[Risk Management]] and [[Continuous Improvement]] helps prioritize across audit cycles.

04-Audit-Concepts/Management Response.md.title: Management Response
04-Audit-Concepts/Management Response.md.body:
**Management response** is management’s formal reaction to audit [[Finding]]s and [[Recommendation]]s, typically included in or appended to the audit report. Responses may agree, partially agree, or disagree, and should explain rationale, planned actions, target dates, and responsible officials. They demonstrate accountability and create a baseline for [[Follow-up]].

Effective responses address root cause, not only immediate correction. They may accept risk where remediation is disproportionate, subject to governance approval and documented rationale. Disagreements should be factual and specific so readers can assess whether the audit conclusion or management position is more persuasive.

In public sector practice, responses are often reviewed by senior management and may be published alongside audit reports for transparency. The response does not replace a [[Management Action Plan]] with detailed milestones, but it should commit to one where complex remediation is required.

Auditors evaluate whether responses are responsive; inadequate responses may elevate follow-up priority or governance escalation paths described in the internal audit charter.

04-Audit-Concepts/Manual Control.md.body:
A **manual control** is performed by people (reviews, approvals, reconciliations, access certifications). OE evidence often includes signed worksheets, tickets, and reviewer identity. Manual controls are prone to inconsistency; over-reliance without monitoring is a common review theme ([[Control]]).

Access examples: [[Access Approval]] (at grant) vs [[Periodic Access Review]] / access certification (recurring). Also [[Log Review]], [[Exception Report Review]], and [[Manual Override Approval]].

04-Audit-Concepts/Materiality.md.title: Materiality
04-Audit-Concepts/Materiality.md.body:
**Materiality** is the threshold of importance—quantitative or qualitative—at which a misstatement, control gap, or analytical difference could influence the decisions of intended users or the elevation of a [[Finding]]. It connects [[Risk Assessment]], [[Consequence or Impact]], and [[Operational Significance]].

There is **no** universal numeric materiality percentage in this vault and none is asserted as CRA policy. Apply [[Professional Judgment]] relative to the [[Audit Objective]] and [[Criteria]].

Uses: sample design focus; which [[Outlier Analysis|outliers]]/trends to investigate deeply; whether a statistically detectable difference warrants reporting ([[Statistical Significance]] ≠ automatic materiality).

04-Audit-Concepts/Methodology.md.title: Methodology
04-Audit-Concepts/Methodology.md.body:
**Methodology** describes the audit approach: how planning, fieldwork, analysis, and reporting will achieve the [[Audit Objective]] within [[Scope]] against stated [[Criteria]]. It includes risk assessment procedures, control evaluation techniques, sampling or full-population testing choices, use of analytics, and quality assurance steps.

Methodology should be proportionate to engagement risk and complexity. A compliance review may emphasize inspection of authorizations; an IT audit may include [[Configuration Review]] and vulnerability management testing; a performance audit may combine [[Document Review]], interviews, and statistical analysis of [[Structured Data]].

Documented methodology supports reproducibility, peer review, and defensibility of [[Evidence]] and [[Finding]]s. Changes during the engagement (e.g., expanded analytics after preliminary results) should be recorded. [[Sampling Risk]] and limitations from data cut-offs ([[Assessment Cut-Off Date]]) should be explicit in design.

Methodology connects to related **methods** notes in case studies when specific techniques (e.g., [[Walkthrough]], data mining) are applied. A [[Walkthrough]] supports understanding of [[Design Effectiveness]]; it is not by itself [[Operating Effectiveness]] testing for the full [[Audit Period]]. See [[Control Testing]].

04-Audit-Concepts/Operating Effectivenes.title: Operating Effectiveness
04-Audit-Concepts/Operating Effectivenes.body:
**Operating effectiveness** asks whether the [[Control]] **actually performed** as required:

- by the appropriate person or system;
- at the required [[Control Frequency]];
- during the relevant [[Audit Period]];
- with sufficient [[Evidence]];
- consistently enough to support the conclusion.

**Inquiry alone does not demonstrate operating effectiveness** for the period—corroborate ([[Evidence]], [[Inquiry]]). One successful instance does not prove the whole period ([[Sampling Risk]], [[Control Frequency]]). Pre-production testing does not prove production OE for the period ([[Control Implementation]]).

For [[Automated Control]]s: confirm production enablement across the period, inspect in-period [[Change Management|changes]], use [[Audit Logging]] / transactions / [[Exception Testing]], [[Reperformance]] or [[Full-Population Analysis]] as appropriate, and consider ITGCs (access, change) under [[IT Controls]]. Include exception/override paths ([[Manual Overrides]]) and outcome errors ([[False Positives]], [[False Negatives]]).

**Professional judgment** is the application of relevant knowledge and experience to decide scope emphasis, evidence sufficiency, finding elevation/aggregation, wording, and whether cause is supported. Judgment does not replace [[Evidence]] or [[Criteria]]; it operates within them and should be documentable.

04-Audit-Concepts/Recommendation.md.title: Recommendation
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
04-Audit-Concepts/Recommendation.md.body:
A **recommendation** is auditor guidance on actions management should consider to address a [[Finding]], reduce [[Risk]], or strengthen [[Control]]s relative to [[Criteria]]. Good recommendations are specific, actionable, feasible, and linked to root cause rather than symptoms. They should identify who should act (often via [[Control Ownership]] or process owners) without usurping management’s responsibility to decide how to run the organization.

Recommendations vary in urgency and may include short-term compensating actions and longer-term structural fixes. Auditors may offer alternative approaches when trade-offs exist (cost, operational impact, technology constraints). Where management disagrees, responses are captured in [[Management Response]] rather than silently dropping the issue.

Internal audit standards emphasize that recommendations are advisory; implementation choices belong to management and governance. [[Follow-up]] audits verify whether agreed actions were implemented and whether risk was reduced as intended.

Recommendations should avoid vague language (“improve monitoring”) in favor of measurable outcomes (“implement quarterly access reviews for privileged accounts with documented sign-off”—see [[Periodic Access Review]]).

04-Audit-Concepts/Risk.md.title: Risk
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
04-Audit-Concepts/Risk.md.body:
In audit and assurance, **risk** is the possibility that events or conditions will adversely affect the achievement of objectives. Auditors consider inherent risk (before controls), control risk (that controls will not prevent or detect issues), and detection risk (that audit procedures will not detect material misstatements or significant weaknesses). Risk thinking prioritizes where limited audit resources should focus.

Risk is often described in terms of likelihood and impact on objectives such as financial reporting, compliance, operations, reputation, or public trust. Enterprise risk management frameworks categorize strategic, operational, financial, and compliance risks. Internal audit uses risk assessment to build annual plans and to scope individual engagements.

Audit findings frequently express **residual risk**—the risk remaining after considering the effectiveness of existing [[Control]]s—or the risk implied by a gap between condition and [[Criteria]]. Not every control weakness constitutes a reportable finding; significance depends on context, aggregation, and tolerance set by governance.

Linking risk to root cause and effect helps management and those charged with governance decide on [[Recommendation]]s and [[Management Action Plan]] priorities. See also [[Risk Management]] and [[Sampling Risk]] for related ideas.

**Discipline:** do not invent causes the public report does not support. If cause is unknown, say so. Unsupported assumptions are not root causes.

04-Audit-Concepts/Sample Selection.md.title: Sample Selection
04-Audit-Concepts/Sample Selection.md.body:
**Sample selection** designs which items from the [[Sampling Frame]] are tested. **First** reconcile the frame to the [[Intended Population]] ([[Population Completeness]], [[Data Reconciliation]])—or document a scope limitation—then choose a method:

| Method | Selection basis | Representativeness | Population-wide [[Statistical Extrapolation]] |
|---|---|---|---|
| [[Random Sampling]] | Known chance within frame | Designed for frame | May support when design allows |
| [[Stratified Sampling]] | Partition; sample within strata | Improves coverage of segments | May support within design bounds |
| [[Judgmental Sampling]] / [[Risk-Based Selection]] | Deliberate risk/material picks | Not statistical | **Normally unsupported**—item/scoped conclusions only |

Manage [[Sampling Risk]] via design, size, and coverage across the [[Audit Period]] / [[Control Frequency]]. Non-representative convenience samples increase risk. There is **no** universal sample-size formula in this vault; apply [[Materiality]] and [[Risk Assessment]]. For automated controls, consider stratifying by rule version, period slice, and high-risk types. Prefer [[Full-Population Analysis]] when data allow and residual data risks are acceptable.

04-Audit-Concepts/Sampling Risk.md.title: Sampling Risk
04-Audit-Concepts/Sampling Risk.md.body:
**Sampling risk** is the risk that conclusions drawn from a sample differ from what would be concluded if the entire population were tested. Separate:

1. **Sampling variability** — chance difference under a valid statistical design ([[Random Sampling]], [[Stratified Sampling]] on a sound [[Sampling Frame]]).
2. **[[Selection Bias]]** — systematic distortion from how the frame or sample was created (filters, convenience, survivorship)—not cured by looking “random” inside a bad frame.

Auditors manage sampling risk through sample design, size, and evaluation of exceptions. Non-representative selection (convenience or bias toward known problems) increases risk beyond formal statistical formulas.

**[[Statistical Extrapolation]] / projection with stated confidence applies to statistical designs.** [[Judgmental Sampling]] and convenience samples normally support only item-level or scoped conclusions—not population-wide rates. Reports should state when findings are sample-based and whether results were projected.

Some engagements use [[Full-Population Analysis]] when data allow ([[Analytics]] on [[Structured Data]]), **reducing** sampling risk but **not eliminating** audit risk—[[Data Quality]], [[Population Completeness]], query logic, and interpretation remain. In very large datasets, tiny differences may be statistically detectable yet operationally trivial ([[Statistical Significance]], [[Operational Significance]], [[Effect Size]]). [[Missing Data]] in the frame or key fields can make a sample non-representative. Sparse cells raise risk ([[Small-Cell Analysis]]).

04-Audit-Concepts/Scope.md.title: Scope
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence

04-Audit-Concepts/Scope.md.body:
**Scope** defines the boundaries of an audit: which entities, processes, systems, time periods, locations, and activities are included—and explicitly what is excluded. Scope sets expectations for stakeholders about the depth and breadth of examination and prevents misunderstandings about what was and was not reviewed.

Scoping decisions reflect the audit objective, available resources, risk prioritization, and materiality to the organization. Limitations on scope (e.g., restricted access to data, systems not in production, or a sample rather than full population) should be documented so readers can interpret findings and conclusions appropriately. Exclusions do not automatically imply those areas are low risk; they may reflect timing, access, or plan constraints.

Scope may evolve during planning as risk assessment refines focus areas. Material changes should be communicated and recorded. In performance and compliance audits, scope often ties to legislative mandates, program boundaries, or control frameworks under review.

Effective scope statements use plain language: named programs or processes, fiscal or calendar periods, geographic or organizational units, and any reliance on third parties or shared services. Scope works with [[Criteria]] and [[Methodology]] to determine what [[Evidence]] is needed.

## Office of Primary Interest (OPI) and audit client

**Content class:** general professional / vault onboarding vocabulary. [[CRA-Acronym-Dictionary]] records **OPI** as the business area primarily responsible for the audited subject. Related teaching term: [[Audit Client]].

In this vault’s public-case practice:

- **OPI / program owner** — area named as primarily responsible for the audited subject (when the report uses that language).
- **MAP / management-action owner** — management area that agrees to and owns corrective action ([[Management Action Plan Owner]]).
- **Publishing assurance branch** — typically [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]; not the OPI.

OPI and MAP owner are often the same area, but confirm each report’s labeled organizational section. Do not infer OPI from topic similarity alone. See [[Ownership and Assurance Roles]].

04-Audit-Concepts/Substantive Testing.md.title: Substantive Testing
04-Audit-Concepts/Substantive Testing.md.body:
# Substantive Testing

**Content class:** general professional knowledge. This note is not a CRA audit manual, prescribed sampling method, or statement about any current CRA control.

Substantive testing obtains evidence directly about whether the subject matter meets the applicable [[Criteria]]. Depending on the objective, it can include inspecting records, testing transactions, reperforming calculations, or analysing a complete population. It is distinct from testing whether a control was designed or operated effectively, although both may contribute to an [[Audit Conclusion]].

The appropriate population, selection method, period, and evidence reliability must be documented. [[Population Completeness]] and [[Sampling Risk]] affect how far a result can be generalized; [[Full-Population Analysis]] reduces sampling risk but does not by itself establish data validity.

04-Audit-Concepts/System-Generated Evide.body:

Reliability depends on access controls, configuration, [[Data Lineage|data lineage]]/extraction logic, [[Change Management]], completeness of feeds, [[Time Synchronization]], and [[Identity Attribution]] ([[Evidence Reliability]], [[IT Controls]], [[Tool Deployment]], [[Population Completeness]], [[Missing Data]], [[Incomplete Audit Logging]]).

Alert counts or dashboard figures alone may be insufficient ([[Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System]] teaching note in vault). Stage reconciliations of totals do not prove field-level [[Data Accuracy]] ([[Data Reconciliation]]).

04-Audit-Concepts/Three Lines Model.md.title: Three Lines Model
04-Audit-Concepts/Three Lines Model.md.body:
The **Three Lines Model** (formerly “Three Lines of Defense”) describes how organizations structure risk management and control accountability. **First line** functions own and manage risks and controls in day-to-day operations. **Second line** functions provide expertise, monitoring, and policy (e.g., risk management, compliance, IT security) to support and challenge the first line. **Third line** internal audit provides independent assurance on governance, risk management, and controls.

The model emphasizes coordination, not rigid silos. Second-line activities (e.g., continuous monitoring) differ from third-line assurance in independence and mandate. Clear roles reduce gaps and duplication—themes related to [[Roles and Responsibilities]] and [[Horizontal Collaboration]].

Internal audit reports to those charged with governance to preserve independence while working constructively with management. The model aligns with [[Governance]] and [[Risk Management]] expectations in public and private sectors.

Auditors use the model to scope reliance on second-line work, assess control ownership, and frame [[Finding]]s without blurring accountability between lines.

05-Software-Concepts/Access Review Testi.title: Access Review Testing
05-Software-Concepts/Access Review Testi.body:
**Access review testing** is the auditor’s procedure set to evaluate design and [[Operating Effectiveness]] of [[Access Approval]] and [[Periodic Access Review]] (and related joiner–mover–leaver controls).

Typical steps: define complete privileged/user population ([[User Access Dataset]], [[Population Completeness]]); sample grants for approval evidence; sample review cycles for reviewer authority, completeness, timeliness, and follow-up removals; compare to employment/role information via [[Joiner-Mover-Leaver]]; use [[Analytics]] for orphans, unused privilege, and SoD conflicts ([[Sampling Risk]]).

An access listing alone is not sufficient—corroborate with tickets, logs, and review packages ([[Evidence]], [[System-Generated Evidence]]). A signed certification package without entitlement examination or executed removals does **not** demonstrate OE.

05-Software-Concepts/Artificial Intellig.title: Artificial Intelligence
05-Software-Concepts/Artificial Intellig.body:
**Artificial intelligence** refers to systems that perform tasks requiring human-like perception, reasoning, or learning— including machine learning models, large language models, and decision automation. In organizations, AI supports classification, forecasting, natural language interfaces, and operational optimization. AI introduces distinct risks: model bias, drift, opaque reasoning, data leakage, and over-reliance on probabilistic outputs.

Governance spans data suitability ([[Data Quality]]), training and validation documentation, human oversight, security ([[Cybersecurity]]), and alignment with [[Criteria]] and law. AI outputs are generally not standalone audit [[Evidence]] without validation against source data and controls.

[[Risk Algorithms]] used in compliance or prioritization contexts may warrant heightened review for fairness, explainability, and [[Population Completeness]]. [[Tool Acquisition]] and [[Tool Deployment]] processes should cover model lifecycle and monitoring.

Auditors and evaluators increasingly examine whether AI use is documented, authorized, and monitored— themes that case studies may explore when tied to public sources.

Governance matters: without [[Business Intelligence Governance]], divergent definitions (“multiple versions of truth”) undermine [[Evidence-Based Decision-Making]]. Access controls, certified datasets, and change management are [[IT Controls]] concerns.

Auditors evaluate data lineage into BI models, who can publish content, and whether public or regulatory [[Performance Reporting]] matches internal dashboards. [[Outdated Analytics]] and [[Duplicate Analytical Work]] often stem from tool sprawl.

05-Software-Concepts/Cybersecurity.md.title: Cybersecurity
05-Software-Concepts/Cybersecurity.md.body:
**Cybersecurity** is the protection of information systems, data, and services from unauthorized access, disruption, modification, or destruction. It spans people, process, and technology: identity management, network security, application security, vulnerability management, incident response, and security awareness. Cyber risk is a subset of enterprise [[Risk]] with high impact potential for confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Organizations typically align programs to frameworks such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) or equivalent national guidance. [[Defence in Depth]] and [[Security Controls]] operationalize strategy. [[Monitoring and Reporting]] provides visibility into threats and control effectiveness.

Auditors examine governance, policy, control design, and operating effectiveness—not merely the presence of tools. [[IT Controls]] map closely to cybersecurity expectations in modern enterprises. Cybersecurity intersects [[Data Governance]] and [[Artificial Intelligence]] as data and models become critical assets.

05-Software-Concepts/Defence in Depth.md.title: Defence in Depth
05-Software-Concepts/Defence in Depth.md.body:
**Defence in depth** (defense in depth) is a security strategy that layers multiple independent [[Control]]s so that failure of one layer does not wholly compromise protection. Layers may include physical security, network segmentation, endpoint protection, identity and access management, application hardening, encryption, and monitoring. The goal is to increase attacker cost and reduce single points of failure.

The approach assumes breaches may occur and emphasizes detection, containment, and recovery—not perimeter-only thinking. It aligns with [[Cybersecurity]] programs and [[Security Controls]] catalogs that span preventive and detective measures.

Auditors assess whether layers are truly independent (shared dependencies can collapse “depth”) and whether gaps exist at integration points (APIs, cloud shared responsibility boundaries, legacy systems). [[Monitoring and Reporting]] is often a critical late layer for identifying successful bypass of earlier controls.

Defence in depth complements least privilege, secure defaults, and change management within [[IT Controls]].

Distinct from “dormant controls” in [[Security Controls]] (unused *controls*, not unused *accounts*).

Controls: inactivity disablement, owner attestation in [[Periodic Access Review]], monitoring of reactivation. Include dormant IDs in [[User Access Dataset]] populations.

05-Software-Concepts/Excessive Privilege.title: Excessive Privileges
05-Software-Concepts/Excessive Privilege.body:
**Excessive privileges** exist when access was granted (or left after a role change) beyond what the duty requires. The login may still be “authorized,” but the entitlement is inappropriate. Distinct from [[Unauthorized Access]] (no valid authorization / prohibited use).

Common causes: privilege creep, shared admin rights, standing elevation, and incomplete leaver/mover processes. Controls: least privilege / [[Role-Based Access Control]], [[Access Approval]], [[Periodic Access Review]], and timely revocation.

[[Tool Deployment]] notes excessive privileges as a deployment risk.

05-Software-Concepts/IT Controls.md.title: IT Controls
05-Software-Concepts/IT Controls.md.body:
**IT controls** are [[Control]]s over information technology general controls (ITGCs) and application controls that support reliable processing, security, and change management. ITGCs commonly include [[Identity and Access Management|access management]], [[Change Management|change/release management]], backup and recovery, job scheduling, and [[Segregation of Duties]] in administrative functions. Application controls enforce [[Automated Business Rules|business rules]] at transaction level (validations, approvals, reconciliations)—see [[Automated Control]].

Distinguish [[Excessive Privileges]] from [[Unauthorized Access]] when testing access. Weak ITGCs can undermine many application controls simultaneously— a central theme in IT audit. COBIT and similar frameworks organize IT governance and management objectives; [[Security Controls]] address confidentiality, integrity, and availability specifically.

Auditors often test ITGCs before relying on automated application controls or [[Analytics]] over [[Structured Data]]. [[Tool Deployment]] and [[Tool Acquisition]] processes are evaluated for governance and security integration. Pipeline reliability also depends on change and access over jobs/datasets ([[Data Pipeline]]).

IT controls connect to [[Three Lines Model]] roles: operations runs controls, IT security and enterprise architecture provide second-line guidance, internal audit provides assurance.

05-Software-Concepts/Identity and Access.body:
**Identity and access management (IAM)** is the set of processes and technology that identify users and services, authenticate them, authorize access, and manage the lifecycle of identities (joiners, movers, leavers). IAM underpins least privilege and [[Role-Based Access Control]].

Auditors examine whether identities are unique and attributable, whether privileges match duties, and whether joiner–mover–leaver processes prevent orphan or excessive access ([[Privileged Access]], [[Access Approval]], [[Periodic Access Review]]).

Do **not** invent CRA-specific IAM product names or claim current CRA access-control weakness without a public source.

Causes include filters, failed loads, disabled logging, truncated retention, or missing identity/timestamp fields ([[Missing Data]], [[Population Completeness]]).

05-Software-Concepts/Manual Overrides.md.title: Manual Overrides
05-Software-Concepts/Manual Overrides.md.body:

Risk is **uncontrolled** or [[Unmonitored Manual Overrides|unmonitored]] override use—not the mere existence of an override path. Do **not** assume every override is improper. Do **not** invent CRA override UIs; EFMS public scope is detection alerting, not a published transactional-override audit.

05-Software-Concepts/Monitoring and Repo.title: Monitoring and Reporting
05-Software-Concepts/Monitoring and Repo.body:
**Monitoring and reporting** in IT and security contexts means continuous or periodic observation of systems, controls, and events, followed by analysis and communication to stakeholders. Security monitoring includes log aggregation, SIEM correlation, vulnerability scanning, and threat intelligence. Operational monitoring covers performance, availability, and capacity.

For onboarding clarity: [[Audit Logging|log generation]] ≠ [[Monitoring and Alerting|alerting]] ≠ [[Log Review|periodic log review]] ≠ [[Exception Report Review]]. Effective monitoring defines what to measure, thresholds, escalation paths, and [[Data Retention|retention]] aligned with [[Criteria]] and policy. Reporting translates metrics and incidents into governance-ready information— dashboards, exception reports, and post-incident reviews. Without actionable reporting, monitoring becomes noise.

Auditors examine whether monitoring covers critical assets and [[Privileged Access Monitoring|privileged activity]], whether alerts are triaged timely, and whether reports reach accountable roles. Gaps often appear in cloud workloads, legacy apps, or [[Unstructured Information]] stores.

Monitoring supports [[Cybersecurity]] detect/respond functions and feeds [[Performance Reporting]] and [[Business Intelligence]] when operational data is reused for management insight.

outgoing_links: How Access Control Relates to Segregation of Duties
05-Software-Concepts/Periodic Access Rev.body:
**Periodic access review** (access certification) is a **detective** control: on a defined frequency, an appropriate reviewer examines whether retained access remains necessary and documents keep/remove decisions. Distinct from [[Access Approval]] at grant time.

[[Recommendation]] uses “quarterly access reviews for privileged accounts with documented sign-off” as a measurable-recommendation example. **Documented sign-off is not sufficient** without evidence that entitlements were examined and that remove decisions were executed ([[Operating Effectiveness]], [[Document Review]], [[Access Review Testing]]). [[Control Ownership]] notes reviews lapse without ownership. Population must be complete ([[User Access Dataset]], [[Population Completeness]]); include [[Joiner-Mover-Leaver]] outcomes.
