05-Software-Concepts/Privileged Access.m.title: Privileged Access
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
05-Software-Concepts/Privileged Access.m.body:
**Privileged access** is elevated technical or administrative capability beyond ordinary end-user permissions (e.g., administrator, DBA, security-admin, break-glass, highly elevated application roles). It is more sensitive because it can change configurations, identities, logs, or large data populations.

Distinct from ordinary user access and from [[Excessive Privileges]] (too much entitlement for a duty) and [[Unauthorized Access]] (use without valid authorization). Include human admins, [[Service Accounts]], and [[Dormant Accounts]] still enabled when scoping populations ([[User Access Dataset]], [[Population Completeness]]).

Path (teaching): Privileged Access → risk → [[Access Approval]] / [[Segregation of Duties]] → [[Periodic Access Review]] / [[Privileged Access Monitoring]] → [[Access Review Testing]] → [[Evidence]].

05-Software-Concepts/Security Controls.m.title: Security Controls
05-Software-Concepts/Security Controls.m.body:
**Security controls** are safeguards prescribed to meet security [[Criteria]] and reduce [[Risk]] to information assets. They include administrative controls (policies, training), technical controls (firewalls, MFA, encryption), and physical controls (badges, secure facilities). Frameworks such as NIST SP 800-53 and ISO 27001 annexes provide structured control baselines that organizations tailor via risk assessment.

Controls are selected based on asset value, threats, vulnerabilities, and regulatory obligations. Implementation requires [[Control Ownership]], configuration management, and periodic testing. Compensating controls may address gaps when primary controls cannot be deployed immediately.

Auditors map controls to risks and evaluate design and operation. Overlapping controls may indicate [[Defence in Depth]]; missing or dormant controls (e.g., logging not reviewed) are common review themes. Security controls intersect [[IT Controls]] and broader [[Governance]].

Cloud and SaaS environments require explicit shared-responsibility clarity— which party implements which controls.

05-Software-Concepts/Structured Data.md.title: Structured Data
05-Software-Concepts/Structured Data.md.body:
**Structured data** is information organized in defined fields and records— relational tables, spreadsheets with consistent columns, JSON with schemas, or log formats— suitable for querying, joining, and automated analysis. Structure enables [[Analytics]], population testing, and validation rules that support [[Evidence]] in audits.

Quality dimensions ([[Data Quality]], completeness, timeliness) still apply; structure does not imply [[Data Accuracy|accuracy]]. [[Data Lineage|Lineage]] from source systems through [[Data Pipeline|ETL]] to reporting layers affects [[Evidence Reliability]]. Auditors often request extracts with documented definitions and [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]] alignment.

Structured data contrasts with [[Unstructured Information]] (narrative documents, email bodies, images), which may require text mining or manual review. Many audits combine both.

Governance under [[Data Governance]] and [[Information and Data Strategy]] defines ownership, standards, and access for structured enterprise data.

05-Software-Concepts/System Configuratio.body:
**System configuration** is the set of parameters, flags, and rule objects that determine runtime behaviour—distinct from source code and from the approved business requirement. Configuration drift can make a well-designed control fail in production.

Test with [[Configuration Review]]; control changes via [[Change Management]] / [[Deployment Approval]]. Public EFMS report does **not** disclose protected configuration details.

05-Software-Concepts/Time Synchronizatio.title: Time Synchronization
05-Software-Concepts/Time Synchronizatio.body:
**Time synchronization** keeps system clocks aligned so event order across hosts is trustworthy. Skew breaks sequencing of overrides, access changes, and failures and weakens log-based [[Evidence Reliability]] / [[System-Generated Evidence]].

05-Software-Concepts/Tool Acquisition.md.title: Tool Acquisition
05-Software-Concepts/Tool Acquisition.md.body:
**Tool acquisition** is the process of selecting and procuring software, platforms, or technology services to meet business needs. It typically includes requirements definition, market research, security and privacy assessment, contract negotiation, licensing, and alignment with enterprise architecture and [[Information and Data Strategy]]. Public sector acquisition often follows formal procurement rules and fairness principles.

Risk areas include vendor lock-in, unclear data residency, inadequate SLAs, and shadow IT when acquisition bypasses governance. Security reviews should map vendor controls to organizational [[Criteria]] before [[Tool Deployment]].

Auditors examine whether acquisition documented alternatives, involved [[Cybersecurity]] and legal review, and established ownership for ongoing [[Monitoring and Reporting]] and patch management.

Acquisition connects to [[Business Intelligence Tools]] and [[Artificial Intelligence]] when organizations buy analytics or model-hosting capabilities.

05-Software-Concepts/Tool Deployment.md.title: Tool Deployment
05-Software-Concepts/Tool Deployment.md.body:
**Tool deployment** covers installing, configuring, integrating, and releasing technology into production (or controlled pilot) environments. It includes [[Change Management]], testing, rollback plans, identity provisioning, and documentation. Secure deployment applies hardening baselines, secrets management, and network placement consistent with [[Defence in Depth]].

Weak deployment practices— [[Excessive Privileges]], default credentials, missing logging, or unpatched dependencies— create immediate [[Risk]]. [[IT Controls]] over change and release management are standard audit focus areas. [[Deployment Approval]] should be distinct from the builder; [[Code Review]] is a common quality gate.

Deployment should follow outputs of [[Tool Acquisition]]: approved architecture, data flows, and operational runbooks. Post-deployment, [[Monitoring and Reporting]] / [[Control Ownership]] validate availability, security signals, and that controls still meet objectives—not only that the release succeeded.

Agile and continuous delivery increase deployment frequency; governance shifts toward automated pipelines, policy-as-code, and [[Segregation of Duties]] in CI/CD.

05-Software-Concepts/Transactional Datas.title: Transactional Dataset
05-Software-Concepts/Transactional Datas.body:
A **transactional dataset** holds event-level records (claims, payments, access events) used as pipeline inputs or as a candidate [[Retrieved Population]] for analysis. Structure enables [[Analytics]]; quality dimensions still apply ([[Data Quality]]).

A received transactional extract is **not** automatically the [[Intended Population]] / [[Audit Population]]—assess [[Population Completeness]] and [[Inclusion and Exclusion Rules]] before drawing population-level conclusions.

05-Software-Concepts/Unauthorized Access.title: Unauthorized Access
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
05-Software-Concepts/Unauthorized Access.body:
**Unauthorized access** is access or use without valid authorization—never approved, revoked but still active, credential misuse, or policy-prohibited use. Distinct from [[Excessive Privileges]] (authorized but too broad).

**Official public CRA context (EFMS):** [[Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System]] states EFMS was implemented to reduce risks of unauthorized employee access to taxpayer information and uses audit trails and business rules to identify questionable activity. That is a **detective monitoring** case theme—not a public finding that CRA privileged-access provisioning is weak.

05-Software-Concepts/Unauthorized System.title: Unauthorized System Changes
05-Software-Concepts/Unauthorized System.body:
**Unauthorized system changes** are modifications to code, configuration, rules, or pipelines without required approval or outside the change process. They break the link between business intent and technical reality and undermine automated-control reliance.

Related EFMS public theme: ad hoc rule changes / incomplete history—use as teaching context only; do not invent current CRA enterprise change failures.

05-Software-Concepts/Unstructured Inform.title: Unstructured Information
05-Software-Concepts/Unstructured Inform.body:
**Unstructured information** lacks a fixed schema: correspondence, policy PDFs, scanned forms, chat logs, web content, and multimedia. It carries substantial operational and legal value but is harder to search, classify, and analyze at scale than [[Structured Data]]. Retention, privacy, and discovery obligations still apply.

Organizations manage unstructured content through document management systems, records classification, and search tools. [[Artificial Intelligence]] and modern search can extract entities and themes but introduce validation needs— outputs are not automatic [[Evidence]] without corroboration.

Auditors review whether critical controls (approvals, contracts, security exceptions) are documented in retrievable form and whether retention policies are enforced. [[Siloed Knowledge]] in personal drives or mailboxes is a recurring risk theme.

Linking unstructured sources to structured transactions (metadata, case IDs) improves traceability for investigations and audits.

05-Software-Concepts/User Access Dataset.title: User Access Dataset
05-Software-Concepts/User Access Dataset.body:
A **user access dataset** is the structured extract of identities and entitlements used for access analytics and [[Access Review Testing]]. Expected elements typically include identity ID, account type (human/[[Service Accounts]]/shared), roles/groups, privileges, owner, last use, status, and source system.

**Completeness:** reconcile to directory/PAM/application admin stores; include nested group memberships, admin, break-glass, [[Dormant Accounts]], and service accounts. Incomplete frames inflate [[Sampling Risk]] ([[Population Completeness]], [[Missing Data]]).

A listing shows entitlement, not appropriate use—pair with [[Audit Logging]] / [[Privileged Access Monitoring]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Analytical V.title: Analytical Validity
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Analytical V.body:
**Analytical validity** means the method, population, assumptions, and interpretation appropriately answer the audit question. Distinct from [[Reproducibility]]:

```text
Reproducible → same inputs + method → same result
Valid → result is fit to support the conclusion for the objective/criteria
```

Invalid-but-reproducible examples: complete analysis of the wrong [[Retrieved Population]]; reproducible association misread as causation; reproducible filter that silently applies [[Systematic Exclusion]].

Judge validity with [[Population Completeness]], [[Data Quality]], [[Criteria]], [[Professional Judgment]], and [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Analytics.md.title: Analytics
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Analytics.md.body:
**Analytics** is the systematic analysis of data to discover patterns, test hypotheses, and support decisions. It ranges from [[Descriptive Statistics|descriptive]] (what happened) to diagnostic (why), predictive (what may happen), and prescriptive (what to do). In audit, analytics can support [[Full-Population Analysis]], [[Outlier Analysis]], [[Trend Analysis]], profile [[Risk]], and enhance [[Methodology]] efficiency.

Analytics quality hinges on [[Structured Data]] fitness, documented logic, [[Reproducibility]], [[Analytical Validity]], and analyst competence. Results should distinguish statistical association from causation unless [[Research]] methods support causal claims. **Reproducible ≠ valid**—wrong population or logic can reproduce a wrong answer.

In very large datasets, statistically detectable differences may be operationally negligible—apply [[Materiality]], [[Effect Size]], and [[Operational Significance]]. Organizational challenges include [[Outdated Analytics]], tool fragmentation, and [[Siloed Knowledge]].

Document sources, extract dates, scripts/parameters/versions, transforms, inclusion/exclusion rules, and limitations ([[Reproducibility]], [[Sampling Risk]], [[Data Suppression]], [[Rounding]]) when findings depend on analytical output. Prefer independent review or [[Reperformance]] of critical analytics.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Assessment C.title: Assessment Cut-Off Date — Audit Application
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Assessment C.body:
An **assessment cut-off date** is the point in time through which transactions or records are included in an assessment, audit test, or statistical estimate. Events after cut-off belong to subsequent periods. Cut-off is fundamental to fairness of [[Performance Reporting]], tax or benefit processing reviews, and financial-style testing.

Misapplied cut-off causes [[Population Completeness]] issues and distorts trends when compared across periods. Auditors perform cut-off tests near period-end to verify recording in correct periods.

In dynamic systems, late-arriving data may require [[Reassessment Data]] or [[Statistical Revision]]. Reports should state cut-off explicitly so readers do not assume real-time completeness.

Link to [[Initial Assessment Data]] when first-pass populations are frozen before later updates.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Audit Popula.title: Audit Population
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Audit Popula.body:
The **audit population** is the set of items (records, transactions, accounts, cases, or events) about which the engagement intends to draw conclusions for the [[Audit Objective]] within [[Scope]] and [[Audit Period]] against [[Criteria]].

Keep layers distinct:

| Layer | Meaning |
|---|---|
| [[Intended Population]] | All items that belong given objective, scope, period, criteria, and [[Inclusion and Exclusion Rules]] |
| [[Retrieved Population]] | Items actually obtained in extracts, registers, or reports |
| [[Sampling Frame]] | List/dataset from which a sample is drawn—should match the intended population |
| Sample | Items selected for testing ([[Sample Selection]]) |

Do **not** treat a received dataset as the audit population until [[Population Completeness]] is assessed. [[Transactional Dataset|Transactional datasets]] are common inputs; they are not automatically the intended population.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Business Int.title: Business Intelligence Governance
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Business Int.body:
**Business intelligence governance** defines roles, standards, and processes for official metrics, dashboards, and semantic models. It answers who may publish data products, how definitions are approved, how changes are versioned, and how access is controlled. Strong BI governance reduces conflicting KPIs and supports [[Evidence-Based Decision-Making]].

Elements often include a metric registry, data stewardship, promotion workflows from sandbox to production, and alignment with [[Information and Data Strategy]]. [[Chief Data Officer]] functions frequently sponsor or chair BI governance forums.

Auditors review whether reported performance in audits matches “certified” BI definitions and whether ad hoc reports drove decisions without control. Weak governance contributes to [[Outdated Analytics]] and misstated [[Performance Reporting]].

BI governance sits within broader [[Data Governance]] and [[IT Controls]] (access, change management).

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Business Int.title: Business Intelligence
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Business Int.body:
**Business intelligence** (BI) is the discipline of turning organizational data into actionable insight for planning and operations. It combines data integration, modeling, reporting, and visualization so leaders can monitor [[Enterprise Objectives]] and performance. BI emphasizes recurring metrics and dashboards, often built on curated datasets rather than one-off analyses.

BI success depends on [[Data Governance]], consistent definitions, and [[Business Intelligence Governance]] that certifies official metrics. Without governance, parallel spreadsheets and [[Duplicate Analytical Work]] proliferate.

BI complements [[Analytics]] and [[Research]]: BI tends toward standardized KPIs; analytics may explore hypotheses; research may investigate causality or program theory. [[Business Intelligence Tools]] implement BI capabilities technically.

Auditors use BI outputs cautiously as [[Evidence]]— verifying lineage, [[Data Quality]], and alignment with [[Performance Reporting]] to external stakeholders.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Chief Data O.title: Chief Data Officer
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Chief Data O.body:
The **chief data officer** (CDO) is a senior role accountable for enterprise data strategy, [[Data Governance]], and value realization from data assets— often partnering with CIO, CISO, and program leaders. Responsibilities may include standards, quality programs, metadata, analytics priorities, and culture for [[Evidence-Based Decision-Making]].

CDO authority varies: some organizations grant budget and policy power; others are coordinating roles. Success requires clear [[Roles and Responsibilities]] relative to IT operations and security.

Auditors examine whether governance forums exist, issues escalate, and [[Information and Data Strategy]] is operational—not only whether a CDO title is filled.

Public sector appointments may be described in official org charts when sourced; no specific incumbent claims appear in this note.

## CRA-specific official placement (not this note’s general definition)

On the CRA Organization baseline, the Assistant Commissioner of [[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch|SIIB]] is also the Chief Data Officer (and Chief Service Officer). That is an **official public CRA organizational fact** on the branch/org notes — distinct from the general CDO concept above. Enterprise CDO placement does **not** make SIIB the data owner of every program dataset. See [[Data Owner]] and [[Ownership and Assurance Roles]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Comparabilit.title: Comparability Across Editions — Audit Application
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Comparabilit.body:
**Comparability across editions** means users can meaningfully compare reports, tables, or indicators over time or between publications. Breaks in comparability arise from definition changes, classification updates, [[Statistical Revision]], [[Rounding]] rule changes, or scope changes in [[Performance Reporting]].

Publishers may provide bridged series, parallel publication of old and new definitions, or marked break points. Without such aids, trend analysis misleads decision-makers and auditors.

When audits benchmark performance year-over-year, verify that KPI definitions and populations remained stable or that adjustments were documented. [[Data Suppression]] changes can also alter apparent trends.

[[Analytics]] projects should store edition metadata alongside datasets to prevent mixing incompatible vintages.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Confidence I.title: Confidence Interval
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Confidence I.body:
A **confidence interval** is a range of plausible values for a population parameter (or projected rate) consistent with the sample/design and stated confidence level. Often more informative for audit communication than a binary significant/non-significant label ([[Statistical Significance]]).

Requires a statistical design and sound [[Sampling Frame]] for [[Statistical Extrapolation]]. Judgmental samples normally do not justify population confidence intervals. Keep case-specific levels (e.g. Audit Yield segment **95%**) bound to their reports—not as a vault-wide rule.

Uncertainty and directional language also appear in [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]] and [[Reasonable Assurance]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Continuous I.title: Continuous Improvement
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Continuous I.body:
**Continuous improvement** is the ongoing cycle of measuring performance, identifying gaps, implementing changes, and verifying results— Plan-Do-Check-Act and related models. In audit contexts, it applies to remediation ([[Management Action Plan]]), audit methodology refinement, and organizational processes under review.

For data and analytics functions, improvement means raising [[Data Quality]], retiring [[Outdated Analytics]], and learning from [[Finding]]s and [[Follow-up]]. Without feedback loops, the same exceptions recur.

Improvement should align with [[Enterprise Objectives]] and be evidenced—not merely aspirational slogans. [[Performance Reporting]] and [[Monitoring and Reporting]] supply metrics for improvement cycles.

Auditors distinguish one-off fixes from sustained capability building when evaluating management responses.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Data Governa.title: Data Governance
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Data Governa.body:
**Data governance** is the exercise of authority and control over data assets— policies, standards, ownership, quality management, lifecycle, privacy, and security. It clarifies [[Roles and Responsibilities]] for data stewards, custodians, and consumers. Effective governance improves [[Data Quality]], lawful use, and trust in [[Analytics]] and [[Business Intelligence]].

Governance bodies prioritize critical data elements, resolve definition disputes, and oversee metadata and lineage. It connects to [[Information and Data Strategy]] and enterprise [[Governance]]. Public sector contexts add transparency, official languages, and statistical publication rules where applicable.

Auditors assess whether governance is operational (decisions documented, issues remediated) or nominal (policies only). Data used as [[Evidence]] should trace to governed sources with known [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]] and quality attributes.

Data governance supports [[Risk Algorithms]] and [[Artificial Intelligence]] by defining training data standards and monitoring responsibilities.

How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance
How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory
Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Data Quality.body:
**Data quality** describes fitness for use across dimensions such as [[Data Accuracy|accuracy]], completeness, consistency, [[Data Timeliness|timeliness]], validity, and [[Record Uniqueness|uniqueness]]. Keep these dimensions distinct—especially accuracy vs completeness. Poor quality undermines [[Analytics]], [[Risk Algorithms]], [[Management Reporting]], and audit [[Evidence]]. Quality is contextual: data adequate for operational processing may be insufficient for statistical publication or forensic audit.

[[Missing Data]] is a primary way completeness fails: expected records, fields, periods, or supporting evidence are absent. That weakness can cascade into [[Population Completeness]] problems and lower [[Evidence Reliability]], so auditors document quality limitations when relying on data extracts and may test quality rules directly.

Management typically combines preventive controls (validations at entry), detective controls (profiling, [[Data Reconciliation|reconciliations]]), and remediation workflows. [[Data Governance]] assigns stewardship and defines critical data elements. Pipeline stages ([[Data Pipeline]]) are common quality failure points (filters, [[Rejected Records]], bad [[Reference Data]]).

Related concepts include [[Population Completeness]], [[Initial Assessment Data]] versus [[Reassessment Data]], and [[Statistical Revision]]. Improving data quality is a [[Continuous Improvement]] theme tied to [[Enterprise Objectives]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Data Suppres.title: Data Suppression — Audit Application
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Data Suppres.body:
**Data suppression** withholds or masks cell values in published tables to reduce re-identification risk or protect confidential business information. Suppression rules often trigger when counts are below thresholds or when dominant contributors could be inferred. It is a standard statistical disclosure control technique alongside [[Rounding]] and aggregation.

Suppression affects [[Comparability Across Editions]] and may limit [[Small-Cell Analysis]]. Users cannot assume missing cells equal zero. Auditors working with public statistics must read methodological notes and not reconstruct suppressed values from other sources inappropriately.

Internal audit datasets may also redact fields for privacy; suppression differs from [[Data Quality]] errors but similarly constrains analysis. Treat suppressed or redacted cells as a distinct form of [[Missing Data]]—intentional and disclosed—not as accidental incompleteness.

Understanding suppression is essential for [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]] when audits reference public aggregate data.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Data Timelin.body:

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Descriptive.title: Descriptive Statistics
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Descriptive.body:
**Descriptive statistics** summarise what happened in a dataset—counts, rates, distributions, concentrations, and simple time profiles—without claiming causal inference. First step in [[Analytics]] profiling for [[Outlier Analysis]], [[Trend Analysis]], and [[Full-Population Analysis]].

Document the [[Retrieved Population]], [[Inclusion and Exclusion Rules]], and limitations ([[Reproducibility]]). Large-N descriptions can still be operationally trivial ([[Operational Significance]], [[Effect Size]]).

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Duplicate An.title: Duplicate Analytical Work
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Duplicate An.body:
**Duplicate analytical work** occurs when multiple teams independently build similar datasets, reports, or models— wasting effort and producing conflicting numbers. Duplication often signals weak [[Business Intelligence Governance]], unclear [[Roles and Responsibilities]], or lack of [[Horizontal Collaboration]].

Duplication increases [[Risk]] that decisions rely on non-certified [[Outdated Analytics]]. Central platforms, reusable data products, and mandate to reuse official metrics reduce duplication.

Auditors may note parallel reporting chains when testing [[Performance Reporting]] consistency. Recommendations often steer toward shared definitions under [[Data Governance]] rather than banning local analysis entirely.

Some duplication is healthy for assurance (independent verification) if roles and methods are explicit.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Effect Size..title: Effect Size
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Effect Size..body:
**Effect size** describes the magnitude of a difference or association (absolute or relative), separate from whether it is statistically detectable. Large samples can yield tiny but “significant” effects; small samples can miss large effects.

Use effect size with [[Materiality]] and [[Operational Significance]] when deciding whether to investigate or report. Pair with [[Confidence Interval]]s where design allows.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Enterprise O.title: Enterprise Objectives
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Enterprise O.body:
**Enterprise objectives** are organization-wide outcomes and priorities— strategic goals, service standards, compliance mandates, and resource stewardship targets. They cascade to programs and metrics used in [[Performance Reporting]] and [[Business Intelligence]]. Clear objectives enable [[Risk Management]] and meaningful [[Criteria]] in audits.

Objectives should be measurable or have observable indicators where possible. Conflicting objectives (e.g., speed versus accuracy) require explicit trade-off governance. [[Information and Data Strategy]] supports objectives with data capabilities; [[Evidence-Based Decision-Making]] depends on aligned metrics.

Auditors map [[Audit Objective]] and scope to enterprise objectives to assess relevance and significance of [[Finding]]s. Changes in corporate plans may shift risk focus across audit cycles.

Public organizations often express objectives in departmental plans and results reports— to be linked via official source notes when available.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Evidence Rel.title: Evidence Reliability
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Evidence Rel.body:
**Evidence reliability** is the extent to which information supports audit conclusions without material misstatement or ambiguity. Reliability increases with independent sources, system integrity, documented lineage, and corroboration; it decreases with manual manipulation, weak access controls, or unknown extraction logic.

For digital [[Evidence]], auditors consider who can alter data, whether logs are protected, and whether analytics scripts are version-controlled ([[Reproducibility]]). [[Data Quality]] and [[Population Completeness]] directly affect reliability; [[Missing Data]] (absent records, fields, periods, or supporting workpapers) is a common reason reliability falls short of the conclusion being drawn. [[Selection Bias]] and incomplete extracts can make results look precise yet unreliable for the [[Intended Population]].

Reliability is judged relative to the [[Audit Objective]] and [[Criteria]]— not absolute truth. A reproducible analysis can still be invalid ([[Analytical Validity]]). [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]] extends reliability to published statistics and estimates and to [[Audit Conclusion]] strength.

Distinguish reliability from relevance: reliable but off-scope data still fails appropriateness tests.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Evidence-Bas.title: Evidence-Based Decision-Making
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Evidence-Bas.body:
**Evidence-based decision-making** uses relevant, reliable information— data, [[Research]], professional judgment, and stakeholder input— to choose actions. It does not mean data alone decides; it means choices are transparent about evidence used and limitations acknowledged.

Enablers include [[Data Quality]], governed [[Business Intelligence]], skilled [[Analytics]], and culture that welcomes disconfirming facts. Barriers include [[Outdated Analytics]], [[Siloed Knowledge]], and pressure for quick answers.

Public sector context adds legal constraints, fairness, and transparency duties. Audit functions contribute evidence on controls and performance but respect management’s decision authority.

Auditors may evaluate whether programs monitor outcomes and adjust based on metrics versus anecdote— without prescribing specific policy choices.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/False Negati.title: False Negatives
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/False Negati.body:
A **false negative** is a failure to flag/block when the rule should have (missed risk). Low override or alert volume is **not** proof of good control—silent misses may not appear in override logs. Pair FP and FN analysis when assessing [[Automated Business Rules]] outcomes.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/False Positi.title: False Positives
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/False Positi.body:
A **false positive** is a rule/alert that fires when it should not (relative to policy intent). High false-positive rates drive legitimate [[Manual Overrides]] and alert fatigue; ignoring them leaves bad rules in place.

**Official EFMS theme:** some rules generated many false-positive alerts; MAP included review of high false-positive rules ([[Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System]]). Alert counts alone are insufficient evidence ([[System-Generated Evidence]]).

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Horizontal C.title: Horizontal Collaboration
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Horizontal C.body:
**Horizontal collaboration** is cooperation across organizational units at similar hierarchy levels— sharing data, methods, and lessons without relying solely on vertical command chains. It improves consistency of [[Analytics]], reduces [[Duplicate Analytical Work]], and spreads good practices for [[Data Governance]] and [[Business Intelligence Governance]].

Enablers include communities of practice, shared platforms, clear [[Roles and Responsibilities]], and psychological safety to ask questions. Barriers include competing priorities, funding silos, and [[Siloed Knowledge]] in local files.

Auditors may observe whether risk and performance insights cross functions or remain trapped in single branches. [[Three Lines Model]] coordination between first and second lines also depends on horizontal habits.

Horizontal collaboration supports [[Continuous Improvement]] and [[Evidence-Based Decision-Making]] at enterprise scale.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/How Statisti.title: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
outgoing_links: How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/How Statisti.body:
Auditors increasingly rely on aggregate statistics, analytics, and sampled data. **Statistical limitations**— revision policy, suppression, rounding, sparse cells, changing definitions, and measurement error— constrain how strongly conclusions may be stated. Professional skepticism requires matching assertion strength to evidence strength.

[[Missing Data]] interacts with these limits: accidental gaps reduce [[Data Quality]] and [[Population Completeness]], while [[Data Suppression]] and redaction withhold values by design. Neither should be treated as identical, but both can force directional rather than precise conclusions.

When audit objectives reference public performance or statistical indicators, teams should read methodological footnotes, understand [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]] and [[Statistical Revision]], and assess [[Comparability Across Editions]]. A variance may reflect data process limits rather than control failure.

Limitations should appear in report scope or methodology sections: what was verified, what was taken from published sources as-is, and where conclusions are directional rather than precise. This reduces overreach and supports defensible [[Finding]] language.

Bridge concept linking [[Evidence Reliability]], [[Data Quality]], and [[Performance Reporting]] to core audit communication duties. Cross-domain consequences: [[How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Inclusion an.title: Inclusion and Exclusion Rules
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Inclusion an.body:
**Inclusion and exclusion rules** define which items belong in the [[Intended Population]] and which are out of scope (categories, statuses, dollar thresholds, channels, periods). Document them in methodology so the [[Sampling Frame]] and analytics filters can be checked against the engagement design ([[Scope]], [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]]).

Silent filters in a [[Data Pipeline]] that do not match documented rules create [[Systematic Exclusion]] and threaten [[Population Completeness]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Information.title: Information and Data Strategy
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Information.body:
An **information and data strategy** articulates how an organization will create, manage, share, and use data and information to achieve [[Enterprise Objectives]]. It typically covers vision, principles, target capabilities, priority use cases, governance, and investment roadmaps— aligned with [[Governance]] and [[Risk Management]].

Strategy connects [[Data Governance]], [[Business Intelligence]], [[Analytics]], [[Cybersecurity]], and architecture choices. Without strategy, tools proliferate via ad hoc [[Tool Acquisition]] and [[Duplicate Analytical Work]] increases.

The [[Chief Data Officer]] or equivalent often leads development and monitoring of the strategy. Auditors may assess whether documented strategy matches observed funding, skills, and outcomes— as general governance themes in engagements.

Official departmental data strategies may be cited from public plans when source notes exist; this concept note stays generic.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Initial Asse.title: Initial Assessment Data — Audit Application
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Initial Asse.body:
**Initial assessment data** is the first snapshot of records or metrics used for a decision, audit fieldwork start, or preliminary statistical release, taken at or before an [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]]. It reflects information available at that moment and may omit late corrections.

Initial data supports timeliness; [[Reassessment Data]] may follow when updates arrive. Users must not treat initial figures as final if the process anticipates revision ([[Statistical Revision]]).

Auditors document whether workpapers used initial or updated extracts and whether differences materially affect [[Finding]]s. [[Data Quality]] at initial capture still matters for downstream rework cost.

Contrast with ad hoc drafts lacking governance— initial assessment should follow defined extraction rules.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Intended Pop.title: Intended Population
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Intended Pop.body:
The **intended population** is every item that should be in scope for the engagement given the [[Audit Objective]], [[Scope]], [[Audit Period]], [[Criteria]], and documented [[Inclusion and Exclusion Rules]].

It is the universe conclusions claim to cover—unless wording is narrowed to a [[Retrieved Population]]. Completeness testing reconciles the retrieved extract to this intended set ([[Population Completeness]], [[Data Reconciliation]]).

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Judgmental S.title: Judgmental Sampling
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Judgmental S.body:
**Judgmental sampling** (directed / purposeful selection) deliberately chooses items using auditor knowledge—unusual amounts, high-risk segments, anomalies from [[Outlier Analysis]], or material items ([[Materiality]], [[Risk-Based Selection]]).

**Value:** efficient for investigating known risks and unusual items; complements statistical samples.

**Critical limit:** judgmental (and convenience) samples are **not** designed for statistical [[Representativeness]]. They normally **do not** support [[Statistical Extrapolation]] to the entire [[Intended Population]]. Projecting error rates as if the sample were random overstates assurance ([[Sampling Risk]]).

Distinct from [[Professional Judgment]] (engagement decisions) and from [[Stratified Sampling]] (partition then sample within strata).

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Missing Data.title: Missing Data
outgoing_links: How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance
How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory
Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Missing Data.body:
**Missing data** is information expected for an analysis, population, record, period, or [[Evidence]] set that is unavailable or absent. Absence may be accidental (extract error, late load, lost field), structural (system never captured the attribute), or intentional and disclosed ([[Data Suppression]], redaction, confidentiality). Auditors treat these causes differently: intentional withholding for privacy is not the same as a quality failure, even when both constrain what can be concluded.

## Types

Distinguish forms of absence before assessing impact (first-class notes: [[Missing Records]], [[Missing Values]], [[Systematic Exclusion]], [[Non-Response or Unavailable Evidence]]):

| Type | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| Missing records | Entire in-scope items never appear in the extract or register ([[Missing Records]]) |
| Missing values within records | Rows exist but critical fields are blank, null, or unusable ([[Missing Values]]) |
| Omitted population segments | Groups, regions, channels, or product lines excluded by filter or join logic ([[Systematic Exclusion]]) |
| Truncated extracts | Cut-off, row limits, or incomplete transfers leave part of the period or inventory out |
| Missing time periods | Gaps in the time series relative to the [[Audit Objective]] and [[Scope]] |
| Missing supporting evidence | Source documents, approvals, logs, or workpapers needed to corroborate data |
| Suppressed or redacted public information | Values withheld under disclosure control or ATIP-style redaction—not equivalent to accidental missingness |

[[Data Suppression]] and published redactions constrain analysis by design; they are not automatically [[Data Quality]] errors. Accidental or uncontrolled missingness is a quality and completeness concern. Both can still force narrower conclusions.

## Audit significance

Typical relationship (not an automatic rule):

```text
Missing data
→ weaker data quality
→ possible population incompleteness
→ increased sampling or analytical risk
→ weaker evidence reliability
→ narrower or more qualified conclusions
```

- Completeness is a core [[Data Quality]] dimension; missingness reduces fitness for use relative to the engagement purpose.
- Systematic omissions, truncation, or filter errors threaten [[Population Completeness]] and can invalidate extrapolations from samples to totals.
- Incomplete populations inflate [[Sampling Risk]]; full-population [[Analytics]] can reduce sampling risk but still fails when completeness or quality is weak.
- [[Evidence Reliability]] falls when lineage, coverage, or corroboration is unknown; digital [[Evidence]] already raises integrity and completeness questions.
- When evidence is incomplete, auditors may scope-limit conclusions or qualify reporting ([[Evidence]]). [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]] requires matching assertion strength to evidence strength.

Actual consequence depends on:

- the [[Audit Objective]] and [[Criteria]];
- materiality and the decision the conclusion supports;
- why the data is missing;
- whether missingness is random or systematic;
- whether alternative evidence exists;
- whether the remaining data still supports the intended conclusion.

There is **no** universal missing-data percentage that automatically requires a qualified conclusion.

## Questions auditors should ask

- What records or fields are missing?
- Why are they missing?
- Is the missingness random or systematic?
- Are particular groups, periods, regions, systems, or transaction types underrepresented?
- Can the population be reconciled to an independent source?
- Is alternative evidence available?
- Does the limitation affect only precision, or does it undermine the validity of the conclusion?
- Should the scope or wording of the conclusion be narrowed?

## Possible procedures

Use procedures already supported by related vault concepts (no separate procedure notes yet):

- **Reconciliation** and comparison to independent totals or control totals ([[Population Completeness]], [[Data Quality]])
- **Data profiling** and detective quality checks ([[Data Quality]], [[Analytics]])
- **Completeness testing** against source counts, hash totals, or independent registers ([[Population Completeness]])
- **Source-to-report tracing** and review of extraction logic ([[Evidence Reliability]], [[Structured Data]])
- **Exception analysis** on full or large populations where tools allow ([[Analytics]], [[Sampling Risk]])
- **Sensitivity analysis** of whether conclusions change when incomplete segments are excluded or bounded ([[Sensitivity Analysis]], [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]])
- Cut-off and period alignment checks ([[Assessment Cut-Off Date]])
- Bias checks: [[Selection Bias]], [[Survivorship Bias]]—**not** assumed for every gap

Document limitations in methodology or scope so [[Finding]] language stays defensible.

## Related public CRA cases

Historical published reports only—findings are not current-state claims.

### What official public reports state

- [[Internal Audit - Charities Audit Process]] — limited/incomplete data dispersed across sources; limited ability to report impartiality across the population; documented reviews/approvals not always complete.
- [[Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory]] — incomplete performance measures and attribution/completeness issues (including resolved-while-unassigned accounts and collapsed inventories).
- [[Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence]] — BI/performance use of data where incomplete or suppressed aggregates remain relevant limits ([[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]]).
- [[Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System]] — re-ingestion/completeness and record timeliness themes; security-related redactions withhold some public detail.
- [[Evaluation - Audit Yield]] — cross-system matching gaps and snapshot/population limits affecting agency-wide automation confidence.

### How this vault interprets relevance (derived)

These cases illustrate why missing or incomplete operational data, incomplete measures, population coverage gaps, transfer/re-ingestion completeness, or withheld public detail can weaken population-level monitoring and the strength of conclusions—without claiming that “missing data” was the report’s formal finding title, or that gaps persist today. See also [[How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Operational.title: Operational Significance
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Operational.body:
**Operational significance** (practical importance) asks whether a result matters materially to program outcomes, compliance, service delivery, financial exposure, security, fairness, workload, or management decision-making.

Distinct from [[Statistical Significance]]. A detectable difference may be operationally trivial; a rare event may be operationally critical without a stable significance test ([[Rare High-Impact Events]], [[Materiality]], [[Consequence or Impact]]).

Elevate [[Finding]]s using [[Criteria]], [[Professional Judgment]], and impact—not p-values alone. “Significant” in [[Evidence Evaluation]] / [[Finding]] means **audit-report** significance, not a statistical test result.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Outdated Ana.title: Outdated Analytics
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Outdated Ana.body:
**Outdated analytics** are reports, scripts, models, or dashboards that no longer reflect current data definitions, systems, regulations, or business rules— yet remain in circulation. They create false confidence and conflict with governed [[Business Intelligence]] products.

Causes include staff turnover without [[Knowledge Continuity]], absent version control, and [[Siloed Knowledge]]. Symptoms: reconciliations that never foot, deprecated fields, or schedules that silently fail.

Governance responses: inventory of analytical assets, ownership, periodic recertification, and decommissioning standards. [[Continuous Improvement]] and [[Business Intelligence Governance]] provide forums to retire stale content.

Auditors flag reliance on uncertified analytics when conclusions depend on them; prefer governed sources with [[Evidence Reliability]] documentation.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Outlier Anal.title: Outlier Analysis
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Outlier Anal.body:
**Outlier analysis** identifies unusual observations relative to a distribution, peer group, or baseline. An **outlier** is unusual—not automatically an error, fraud, or [[Control Deficiency]].

Distinguish:

| Label | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Unusual observation | Statistically or visually atypical |
| Exception | Policy/system exception path ([[Exception Testing]], [[Manual Overrides]]) |
| Error | Incorrect data or incorrect automated decision ([[Data Quality]], [[Incorrect Automated Decisions]]) |
| Legitimate unusual activity | Valid outlier (seasonality, approved exception, false-positive correction) |
| Risk indicator | Signal needing investigation (not proof of misconduct) |
| Confirmed control failure | Conclusion only after evidence vs [[Criteria]] |

**Procedure path:**

```text
Data profiling ([[Descriptive Statistics]], [[Analytics]])
→ identify unusual values
→ verify [[Data Quality]] / [[Population Completeness]]
→ compare with business context
→ inspect supporting [[Evidence]]
→ determine whether exception is legitimate
→ assess control or risk implications ([[Materiality]], [[Operational Significance]])
```

Association ≠ causation ([[Analytics]]). Do not claim an outlier proves misconduct. Supports [[Exception Testing]] and [[Judgmental Sampling]] / [[Risk-Based Selection]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Override Pop.title: Override Population Analytics
outgoing_links: How Manual Overrides Weaken Automated Controls
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Override Pop.body:
**Override population analytics** profiles override/exception events after [[Population Completeness]] of the override frame is tested:

1. Frequency and trends by period/rule/type  
2. Concentration by user, unit, region, case type  
3. Reason-code quality (blank/generic)  
4. Outcomes / dispositions after override  
5. Feedback to rule quality ([[False Positives]] / [[False Negatives]])

High legitimate override volume may signal false-positive pressure—not automatic abuse. Low volume ≠ good control if false negatives are silent. Use [[Full-Population Analysis]] when structured data allow; [[Stratified Sampling]] for deep approval/outcome tests.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Performance.title: Performance Reporting
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Performance.body:
**Performance reporting** communicates results against plans, indicators, and [[Enterprise Objectives]]— internally via dashboards and externally via departmental results reports, statistical publications, or regulatory filings. Reports should define indicators, baselines, targets, and measurement methods clearly.

Public sector performance reporting often links planned results to actual outcomes and explains variances. Quality depends on indicator governance, data timeliness, and consistent methodology across reporting periods ([[Comparability Across Editions]]).

Auditors compare performance claims to underlying [[Evidence]], test calculations, and assess whether known limitations ([[Data Suppression]], [[Rounding]], revisions) are disclosed. Misalignment between internal [[Business Intelligence]] and external reports is a common review theme.

Performance reporting supports accountability and [[Evidence-Based Decision-Making]] when metrics are trustworthy.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Population C.title: Population Completeness
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Population C.body:
**Population completeness** means the [[Retrieved Population]] includes all items that belong in the [[Intended Population]] for the [[Audit Objective]], [[Scope]], and [[Audit Period]]—no systematic omissions, truncation, or filter errors ([[Inclusion and Exclusion Rules]]). Incomplete populations inflate [[Sampling Risk]] and can invalidate [[Statistical Extrapolation]].

[[Missing Data]] often produces those gaps: [[Missing Records]], omitted segments ([[Systematic Exclusion]]), truncated extracts, missing time periods, or entire records never loaded. Completeness checks compare source counts, control totals, hash totals, or independent registers ([[Data Reconciliation]]). Cut-off errors at an [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]] are a frequent cause of gaps between financial and operational data.

**Access and pipeline examples:** [[User Access Dataset]] extracts must include nested groups, [[Service Accounts]], and [[Dormant Accounts]] still enabled; analysing only active/successful items can create [[Survivorship Bias]]. [[Data Pipeline]] filters/rejects can silently drop segments. Completeness is distinct from [[Data Accuracy]].

In statistical agencies and large programs, completeness interacts with coverage studies and late-reported transactions. Auditors state when conclusions apply only to retrieved subsets—never treat the extract as the intended universe without testing. Incomplete populations weaken [[Evidence Reliability]] and force narrower [[Audit Conclusion]]s. Validate the [[Sampling Frame]] before [[Sample Selection]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Random Sampl.title: Random Sampling
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Random Sampl.body:
**Random sampling** selects units from a complete [[Sampling Frame]] so each eligible unit has a known (typically equal) chance of selection, without auditor preference for particular items.

**Assumptions:** frame matches the [[Intended Population]] ([[Population Completeness]]); selection is free of convenience bias. Incomplete frames make even “random-looking” picks non-representative ([[Sampling Risk]]).

**Conclusions:** may support [[Statistical Extrapolation]] / projection when design, size, and evaluation allow—disclose in reporting. Does not remove [[Data Quality]] limits.

**Limitations:** rare high-risk items may be undersampled unless combined with [[Stratified Sampling]] or [[Risk-Based Selection]]; no universal sample-size formula in this vault ([[Control Frequency]] still requires enough instances across the [[Audit Period]]).

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Rare High-Im.title: Rare High-Impact Events
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Rare High-Im.body:
**Rare high-impact events** occur infrequently but carry severe compliance, security, financial, or fairness consequences. Counts may be too small for stable rates or significance tests ([[Small-Cell Analysis]]), yet each event can be operationally decisive ([[Operational Significance]], [[Materiality]]).

Do **not** treat lack of [[Statistical Significance]] as proof of acceptable risk. Prefer certainty testing, [[Risk-Based Selection]], and qualitative evaluation against [[Criteria]]. [[False Negatives]] remind that low alert volume is not proof of good control.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Reassessment.title: Reassessment Data — Audit Application
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Reassessment.body:
**Reassessment data** updates or replaces [[Initial Assessment Data]] after new information, corrections, appeals outcomes, or extended cut-off windows. Reassessment improves accuracy but may change prior conclusions, rankings, or risk scores.

Processes should define triggers for reassessment, roles, and communication to stakeholders who acted on initial figures. Without controls, dual versions circulate and undermine [[Evidence-Based Decision-Making]].

Auditors evaluate whether reassessment controls prevent unauthorized retroactive changes and whether logs support [[Evidence Reliability]]. Performance and compliance reviews may test sample cases through initial and final states.

Reassessment relates to [[Statistical Revision]] in published aggregates and to [[Continuous Improvement]] in operational metrics.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Record Uniqu.title: Record Uniqueness
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Record Uniqu.body:
**Record uniqueness** is the [[Data Quality]] dimension that each real-world entity/event appears once (or as intentionally versioned) in the population. Duplicates from bad keys or joins distort counts and reconciliations.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Representati.title: Representativeness
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Representati.body:
**Representativeness** means the analysed set (frame or sample) reflects the [[Intended Population]] well enough for the inference being drawn. Statistical designs ([[Random Sampling]], [[Stratified Sampling]]) aim at representativeness when the [[Sampling Frame]] is complete.

[[Judgmental Sampling]] and convenience picks are typically **not** representative for population-rate claims. Incomplete frames, [[Selection Bias]], and [[Survivorship Bias]] destroy representativeness even when selection within the retrieved set looks orderly.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Research.md.title: Research
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Research.md.body:
**Research** is structured inquiry to produce reliable knowledge— defining questions, methods, data collection, analysis, and conclusions. In government and audit contexts, research supports program evaluation, policy analysis, and exploratory assurance work distinct from routine [[Analytics]] or [[Business Intelligence]] reporting.

Research designs include surveys, experiments, quasi-experiments, case studies, and mixed methods. Standards emphasize ethics, privacy, reproducibility, and clear limitations. Findings should state uncertainty and avoid overgeneralization from small or biased samples.

[[Internal Audit and Program Evaluation]] functions may use research methods for effectiveness questions while still meeting professional assurance standards where applicable. [[Evidence]] from research must meet [[Evidence Reliability]] expectations when cited in [[Finding]]s.

Research outputs feed [[Evidence-Based Decision-Making]] when communicated with context and caveats.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Retrieved Po.title: Retrieved Population
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Retrieved Po.body:
The **retrieved population** is the set of items actually obtained for analysis—extracts, registers, query results, or reports. It may be smaller than the [[Intended Population]] because of filters, rejects, cut-offs, matching failures, or access limits ([[Missing Data]], [[Rejected Records]]).

[[Full-Population Analysis]] of the retrieved set still requires stating when conclusions apply only to that subset ([[Population Completeness]]).

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Risk Algorit.title: Risk Algorithms
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Risk Algorit.body:
**Risk algorithms** are rules, scoring models, or machine learning systems that rank entities, transactions, or cases by perceived [[Risk]] for prioritization or action. Tax and benefits agencies, financial institutions, and regulators commonly use such models for workload allocation—not necessarily as final legal determinations.

Algorithmic risk systems raise governance questions: data bias, transparency, validation, override processes, and periodic recalibration. Errors can affect fairness and public trust. Reviewers examine documentation, testing results, and [[Monitoring and Reporting]] of model performance drift.

Auditors evaluate controls around model changes, access to parameters, and segregation between developers and operators. Links to [[Artificial Intelligence]], [[Data Quality]], and [[Population Completeness]] are common when training data omit segments of the population.

Concept notes do not describe specific organizational models; case studies may reference publicly documented approaches when sources exist.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Risk-Based S.title: Risk-Based Selection
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Risk-Based S.body:
**Risk-based selection** prioritises items using [[Risk Assessment]] signals—high value, high risk, anomaly scores, or [[Rare High-Impact Events]]—often as [[Judgmental Sampling]] or as a certainty stratum inside [[Stratified Sampling]].

Use to focus limited fieldwork. Do **not** treat risk-based picks alone as statistically representative of the whole population ([[Representativeness]], [[Statistical Extrapolation]]). Pair with random/stratified coverage when population rates are needed.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Roles and Re.title: Roles and Responsibilities
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Roles and Re.body:
**Roles and responsibilities** clarify who is accountable, responsible, consulted, and informed for activities— including [[Control Ownership]], data stewardship, audit response, and analytics publication. Ambiguity leads to control gaps, delayed remediation, and [[Siloed Knowledge]].

Frameworks such as RACI matrices document decisions for complex processes. The [[Three Lines Model]] assigns distinct roles to operational management, oversight functions, and internal audit. [[Chief Data Officer]] and IT security roles exemplify second-line specialization.

Clear roles support [[Governance]], [[Risk Management]], and effective [[Follow-up]] on [[Recommendation]]s. Auditors test whether documented roles match practice (e.g., who approves access, who signs reports).

Enterprise [[Information and Data Strategy]] should align role definitions with actual staffing and committees.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Rounding - A.title: Rounding — Audit Application
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Rounding - A.body:
**Rounding** adjusts numeric values to fixed precision for presentation, storage efficiency, or disclosure control. Published statistics may round counts or dollars to nearest thousand, creating small differences between detail and totals. Rounding is not necessarily error but must be documented so users interpret figures correctly.

Auditors reconciling reports to subledger detail should know rounding conventions to avoid false [[Finding]]s. Combined with [[Data Suppression]], rounded tables may not foot mechanically across dimensions.

In analytics, inconsistent rounding between systems can create reconciliation noise; governance may specify standard precision for [[Performance Reporting]].

Rounding policies should appear in statistical or report footnotes; see [[Comparability Across Editions]] when methods change.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Sampling Fra.title: Sampling Frame
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Sampling Fra.body:
The **sampling frame** is the list or dataset from which sample units are drawn ([[Sample Selection]]). For statistical designs, the frame should correspond to the [[Intended Population]]. Gaps between frame and intended population create [[Selection Bias]] and inflate [[Sampling Risk]] even when selection within the frame looks random.

Validate the frame with [[Population Completeness]] and [[Data Reconciliation]] before selecting items—or document a scope limitation.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Selection Bi.title: Selection Bias
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Selection Bi.body:
**Selection bias** arises when the process that creates, filters, or selects records systematically favours some units, so the analysed group is unrepresentative of the [[Intended Population]]. Examples: voluntary response, filtered extracts, convenience picks, risk-based sets treated as random.

Distinct from **sampling variability** under a valid design ([[Sampling Risk]]): chance error vs systematic distortion from how the frame/sample was built ([[Systematic Exclusion]], [[Data Pipeline]] filters).

Not every instance of [[Missing Data]] creates selection bias—random missingness mainly reduces precision; systematic missingness threatens validity ([[Missing Data]]).

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Sensitivity.title: Sensitivity Analysis
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Sensitivity.body:
**Sensitivity analysis** tests whether conclusions change when incomplete segments are excluded, bounded, or alternately assumed. A mitigation when [[Missing Data]], [[Selection Bias]], or uncertain parameters exist ([[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]], [[Missing Data]] procedures).

Use before strong population-rate claims; document scenarios and resulting wording changes for the [[Audit Conclusion]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Siloed Knowl.title: Siloed Knowledge
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Siloed Knowl.body:
**Siloed knowledge** exists when critical know-how, data definitions, or analytical results remain isolated in teams, personal drives, or legacy systems— unknown or unusable elsewhere. Silos increase [[Risk]] from inconsistent decisions, [[Outdated Analytics]], and loss of expertise ([[Knowledge Continuity]] risks).

Technology alone does not fix silos; [[Governance]], incentives, and [[Horizontal Collaboration]] matter. Documented metadata, shared repositories, and certified BI products counter silo effects for [[Structured Data]]; [[Unstructured Information]] needs records management.

Auditors encounter silos when interviewees contradict each other’s metrics or when the same question requires multiple incompatible extracts. Findings may address documentation, stewardship, or enterprise repositories— framed generally unless case evidence supports specifics.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Small-Cell A.title: Small-Cell Analysis
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Small-Cell A.body:
**Small-cell analysis** examines table cells or subgroups with very few observations. Estimates from small cells have high variance and may violate disclosure rules, triggering [[Data Suppression]]. Inferential statements from tiny samples are fragile and easily distorted by outliers.

Analysts may combine categories, use moving averages, or apply hierarchical models— each with assumptions that must be stated. [[Sampling Risk]] rises when audits sample within sparse strata.

[[Research]] ethics also limit reporting on identifiable small groups. Auditors should avoid over-interpretation when exceptions in small cells drive narrative [[Finding]]s.

Link to [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]] when conclusions rest on sparse data.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Statistical.title: Statistical Extrapolation
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Statistical.body:
**Statistical extrapolation** (projection) extends sample results to a broader population or frame using a statistical design and stated evaluation method. Supported only when selection was statistical (e.g. [[Random Sampling]], [[Stratified Sampling]] on a sound [[Sampling Frame]]) and assumptions hold.

**Unsupported** for [[Judgmental Sampling]], convenience samples, or biased frames—those support item-level or scoped conclusions only ([[Sampling Risk]]). Always disclose whether results were projected.

Do not treat Audit Yield’s report-bound confidence statement as a universal extrapolation rule for all engagements.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Statistical.title: Statistical Revision — Audit Application
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Statistical.body:
**Statistical revision** is the practice of updating previously published estimates when new data, methodology improvements, or error corrections become available. Revisions can shift levels and growth rates; agencies often publish revision policies and vintage charts for transparency.

Revisions differ from routine [[Reassessment Data]] at operational level but share communication challenges. Users comparing time series must align vintages or use consistently revised history ([[Comparability Across Editions]]).

Auditors citing public statistics should note publication date, revision status, and known limitations in [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]]. Treating preliminary releases as final can overstate precision.

Major methodological changes require extra documentation and stakeholder notice.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Statistical.title: Statistical Significance
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Statistical.body:
**Statistical significance** asks whether an observed difference or relationship would be unlikely under a specified statistical model or assumption. It is about **detectability under a model**, not automatic business importance.

This vault does **not** mandate a universal significance level (e.g. p < 0.05) as CRA or engagement policy. Report-bound confidence language in public cases (e.g. Audit Yield **95%** for a **specified segment**) must not be generalized.

In very large datasets, tiny differences can become statistically detectable while remaining negligible for [[Operational Significance]] and [[Materiality]]. Conversely, non-significance does **not** prove absence of risk—especially for [[Rare High-Impact Events]] or small samples ([[Small-Cell Analysis]]).

Prefer [[Confidence Interval]]s and [[Effect Size]] plus [[Professional Judgment]] over a binary significant/non-significant label when wording [[Finding]]s or an [[Audit Conclusion]].

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Stratified S.title: Stratified Sampling
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Stratified S.body:
**Stratified sampling** partitions the [[Sampling Frame]] into strata (e.g. value bands, risk tiers, rule versions, periods) and then samples **within each stratum**—often randomly—to improve [[Representativeness]] or allocate effort to important segments. Stratification is **not** the same as [[Judgmental Sampling]] / picking only high-risk items without within-stratum selection.

High-value or high-risk items may form a certainty stratum (100% tested) while other strata are randomly sampled—see [[Evaluation - Audit Yield]] (official: all files ≥ $5 million plus stratified random sample of others; **95%** confidence for the **sampled segment** only).

Interpret within-stratum results for that stratum; combine across strata only when the design supports it. Sparse strata raise [[Sampling Risk]] ([[Small-Cell Analysis]]). Still depends on [[Population Completeness]] of the frame.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Survivorship.title: Survivorship Bias
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Survivorship.body:
**Survivorship bias** is the distortion from examining only completed, active, successful, or retained cases while excluding failures, withdrawals, rejects, dormant items, or never-loaded records. Outcomes and controls can look stronger than they are in the full cohort.

Adjacent vault themes: include [[Dormant Accounts]] in access extracts; inspect [[Rejected Records]]; do not treat alert-only views as complete detection ([[False Negatives]]). Analysing only open/closed operational files may miss treatment coverage needed for a conclusion—without relabeling public reports as “survivorship” findings unless they use that term.

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Systematic E.title: Systematic Exclusion
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Systematic E.body:
**Systematic exclusion** omits a class of in-scope items by filter, join, status rule, channel, region, or period—producing biased coverage of the [[Intended Population]]. A form of [[Missing Data]] / omitted segments that threatens [[Population Completeness]] and can induce [[Selection Bias]].

Document intended [[Inclusion and Exclusion Rules]]; quantify silent pipeline filters ([[Data Transformation]], [[Rejected Records]]).

06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Trend Analys.title: Trend Analysis
outgoing_links: How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions
06-Data-Statistics-Concepts/Trend Analys.body:
**Trend analysis** examines how metrics or rates change over time. Patterns are hypotheses—not findings—until corroborated ([[Evidence]], [[Analytics]] association ≠ causation).

Before interpreting a break or slope, check context:

- changing definitions ([[Comparability Across Editions]]);
- denominators / population composition;
- [[Assessment Cut-Off Date]] and late data ([[Statistical Revision]]);
- seasonality / calendar operations;
- policy or [[Change Management|system/rule changes]];
- [[Data Quality]] / completeness shifts ([[Missing Data]]).

Misleading trends often reflect process or definition change rather than control failure ([[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]]). Prioritise investigation with [[Materiality]] and [[Operational Significance]].

07-Risk-Controls/Business Process Owner..title: Business Process Owner
outgoing_links: How Organizational Ownership Affects System Accountability
Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
07-Risk-Controls/Business Process Owner..body:
**Content class:** general professional concept. The public CRA Organization page does not use this exact title as a formal org-chart label; in vault practice, accountability often appears as a named program area, OPI, or MAP owner in a published audit.

A **business process owner** is accountable for a defined end-to-end process and its **business outcomes**— not for building every system that supports it. Owners set process requirements, accept residual risk within policy, ensure controls fit the process, and respond when audits find gaps. This differs from [[Technical Support]] (technology delivery) and from [[Control Ownership]] when a single control is owned separately from the whole process.

In public-sector internal audit, the “owner” may be a branch, director general area, or delegated official named in the report. [[CRA-Regions]] may deliver field work while headquarters program areas retain policy or oversight accountability; case language varies.

Worked pattern (case-specific, not a universal CRA rule): [[Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence]] names [[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch|SIIB]] as holding BI activity responsibility and MAP lead, while [[Information Technology Branch|ITB]] delivers BI services— illustrating process accountability separate from technical delivery.

For technology-enabled processes, process owners typically set business requirements and exception/override **policy**, accept residual risk, and ensure monitoring ownership is named—without owning independent assurance ([[How Organizational Ownership Affects System Accountability]]). They do not automatically administer systems ([[System Owner]], [[Technical Support]]) or execute AERB remediation.

07-Risk-Controls/Control Ownership.md.body:
**Content class:** general professional concept ([[Ownership and Assurance Roles]] for how this fits CRA onboarding).

**Control ownership** assigns named individuals or roles accountability for designing, operating, and monitoring specific [[Control]]s— not merely executing tasks but ensuring controls remain fit for purpose as [[Risk]] and systems change. Owners document control activities, perform self-assessments, and remediate gaps.

Without ownership, controls decay, access reviews lapse, and audit [[Recommendation]]s lack sustained fixes. Ownership maps to [[Roles and Responsibilities]] and integrates with [[Risk Management]] registers that list controls mitigating each risk.

IT and security controls often split ownership between business process owners and technical custodians; interfaces must be clear to avoid gaps. [[Management Action Plan]] items should name owners with sufficient authority.

Auditors test whether stated owners understand their controls and evidence operation— a common source of [[Finding]]s when documentation exists but practice differs.

Control ownership commonly spans access ([[Access Approval]], [[Periodic Access Review]]), automated rules and overrides ([[Manual Override Approval]], [[Exception Report Review]]), change ([[Change Approval]]), and reporting reconciliations ([[Data Reconciliation]], [[Management Review]]).

07-Risk-Controls/Data Owner.md.title: Data Owner
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
07-Risk-Controls/Data Owner.md.body:
**Content class:** general professional concept for “data owner” and steward/custodian vocabulary ([[Data Governance]]). **Official public CRA facts** for enterprise data-asset leadership placement ([[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch|SIIB]] manages CRA data and information assets; [[Chief Data Officer]] role tied to SIIB on sourced org/case material)— not a claim that one branch owns every dataset in every program.

A **data owner** (in governance frameworks) is accountable for defined information assets: meaning, quality expectations, lawful use, access rules, and issue escalation. Owners approve definitions and prioritize remediation; **custodians** often implement controls in systems; **stewards** coordinate day-to-day quality. These roles are distinct from [[Technical Support]] (hosting, pipelines) and from [[Internal Audit Independence|internal audit assurance]].

Enterprise **CDO** mandate ≠ sole “data owner” of every analytical dataset a program uses. Program branches remain accountable for their processes and may share BI or operational data under governance frameworks ([[Business Intelligence Governance]]). BI case context: SIIB BI responsibility and CDO as SIIB AC signal data leadership; ITB still delivers BI services.

Auditors test whether ownership is operational (documented decisions, quality fixes) or nominal (policy only)— a common theme in data-heavy [[Finding]]s.

For decision and reporting processes, data ownership should cover critical input fields, reference data, outcome/disposition data, and—where overrides exist—override-event meaning and quality expectations ([[Reference Data]], [[Manual Overrides]], [[Management Reporting]]). Enterprise CDO mandate ≠ owner of every program dataset.

07-Risk-Controls/Governance.md.title: Governance
07-Risk-Controls/Governance.md.body:
**Governance** is the system by which organizations are directed and controlled— defining authority, accountability, oversight, and ethical expectations. It includes boards or equivalent bodies, executive leadership, policies, and assurance functions. Effective governance aligns strategy, [[Risk Management]], and resource use with [[Enterprise Objectives]] and stakeholder interests.

Key themes: clear [[Roles and Responsibilities]], transparency, control over financial and non-financial reporting, and independence of internal audit ([[Three Lines Model]]). [[Control Ownership]] must be embedded in management, not delegated entirely to audit.

Public sector governance adds ministers, legislation, access to information, and value-for-money expectations. Auditors evaluate governance processes as part of many engagements— tone at the top, committee effectiveness, and issue escalation.

Governance connects to [[Data Governance]] and [[Information and Data Strategy]] for data-driven organizations.

07-Risk-Controls/Knowledge Continuity.md.title: Knowledge Continuity
07-Risk-Controls/Knowledge Continuity.md.body:
**Knowledge continuity** is the ability to retain and transfer critical know-how when staff change roles, retire, or leave— so operations, [[Control]]s, and analytics remain effective. Loss of continuity drives [[Siloed Knowledge]], [[Outdated Analytics]], and repeated errors despite prior audit [[Finding]]s.

Practices include documented procedures, cross-training, mentorship, repositories for governed definitions, and succession planning for key [[Control Ownership]] roles. [[Horizontal Collaboration]] spreads expertise beyond single points of failure.

Technology helps but does not replace curation— [[Unstructured Information]] in wikis requires maintenance like code. [[Continuous Improvement]] captures lessons from incidents and audits into accessible playbooks.

Auditors may treat continuity as a risk when specialized systems lack backup expertise or when remediation knowledge walked out the door after [[Follow-up]] closed items.
