07-Risk-Controls/Program Owner.md.title: Program Owner
07-Risk-Controls/Program Owner.md.body:
**Content class:** general professional concept for “program owner”; **official public CRA facts** for how [[CRA-Program-Branches]] vs [[CRA-Corporate-Branches]] are described on the org baseline; **official case-specific** when a published audit names an OPI or MAP owner for that program.

A **program owner** (in governance language) is accountable for a program’s objectives, performance, and sustained compliance with policy— often at headquarters for CRA **program branches** that provide technical and policy support for tax administration programs. Regional delivery through [[CRA-Regions]] can involve the same program without every region being the “owner” in audit report language.

Public audits frequently identify the **Office of Primary Interest (OPI)** or **MAP owner** for the audited subject ([[Audit Client]], [[CRA-Acronym-Dictionary]]). Examples in this vault (each tied to its case, not generalized into reporting lines):

- Collections inventory — [[Collections and Verification Branch|CVB]] as OPI/MAP pattern in ARNI case materials
- Charities audit process — program branch named in charities case org section
- Business intelligence — [[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch|SIIB]] responsibility and MAP lead in BI case

Program ownership is related to but not identical to [[Business Process Owner]]: a program may span several processes; a process may cut across programs with shared [[Technical Support]].

07-Risk-Controls/Risk Management.md.title: Risk Management
07-Risk-Controls/Risk Management.md.body:
**Risk management** is the coordinated activity to identify, assess, treat, monitor, and communicate [[Risk]] relative to objectives. Enterprise risk management integrates risks across strategies, operations, reporting, and compliance. It informs prioritization of [[Control]]s, investments, and audit plans.

Standard process: context setting, identification, analysis, evaluation, treatment (avoid, reduce, share, accept), and monitoring. Risk appetite and tolerance statements translate board intent into operational limits.

The [[Three Lines Model]] places risk ownership in the first line, frameworks and challenge in the second, and independent assurance in internal audit. [[Risk Algorithms]] may automate parts of identification or prioritization with distinct governance needs.

Auditors rely on risk registers and assessments but validate with [[Evidence]]— not assuming documentation equals effective management.

07-Risk-Controls/System Owner.md.title: System Owner
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System
07-Risk-Controls/System Owner.md.body:
**Content class:** general professional concept. CRA public org pages do not standardize “system owner” as a single enterprise title; published audits describe **named maintenance, enhancement, and response roles** instead.

A **system owner** is accountable for a named system’s fitness for purpose— onboarding, rule/configuration governance, performance information, and alignment with policy— distinct from every user of the system and distinct from generic infrastructure operations. Owners may delegate day-to-day work to sections or partners; accountability should still be traceable in audit evidence.

System ownership often **splits** between a business or security custodian and a technical maintainer ([[Control Ownership]], [[IT Controls]]). That split is not an invented org chart; it appears where reports name multiple parties.

**Case-specific illustration (EFMS):** [[Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System]] states that Security Branch IFMS maintains/enhances EFMS and supports developers, while ITB Enterprise Fraud Management Services also maintains EFMS; Security Branch is MAP owner with ITB jointly named for selected remediation. This vault does **not** infer a single “system owner” title above those report statements or add reporting lines between Security Branch and ITB.

07-Risk-Controls/Technical Support.md.title: Technical Support
outgoing_links: Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence
07-Risk-Controls/Technical Support.md.body:
**Content class:** general professional concept for the role type; **official public CRA fact** that [[Information Technology Branch|ITB]] develops, operates, maintains, and evolves CRA IT (branch mandate on org baseline).

**Technical support** means building, operating, evolving, and securing the technology that enables business processes— platforms, integrations, service delivery, and often shared infrastructure. It is **not** the same as [[Business Process Owner|business-process ownership]]: enabling a capability does not automatically make IT accountable for the business outcome or for every MAP lead role in a public audit.

Interns and analysts should avoid statements such as “IT owns the program” when cases only show ITB as **service delivery**, co-chair, co-maintainer, or named collaborator ([[Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence]]: ITB BI service delivery while SIIB holds BI responsibility).

Technical support partners with process and [[System Owner|system accountability]] through governance forums, change management, and [[Control Ownership]] splits (business vs technical custodians). [[Three Lines Model]] first-line operators may include both business units and IT operations depending on the control.

07-Risk-Controls/Unclear Accountability..body:
**Content class:** general professional failure-mode concept.

**Unclear accountability** exists when decision authority, control ownership, or incident response responsibility is ambiguous—so issues fall between [[Business Process Owner]], [[System Owner]], [[Technical Support]], and [[Data Owner]]. Consequences: controls without owners, unapproved rule changes, incomplete post-deployment monitoring, incidents passed between teams without a resolver, duplicated or missing controls, and [[Management Action Plan]] items without accountable owners ([[Control Ownership]], [[Ownership and Assurance Roles]]).

08-Cases/Evaluation - Audit Yield.md.body:
> This note summarizes a publicly released CRA report. It is not an internal working paper, does not contain non-public evidence, and should be read with the original official report.

> **Historical context:** Findings and estimates reflect analysis as of **July 2019** on audit cohorts closed in **FY 2015–16** (GST/HST) and **FY 2016–17** (income tax). Do not treat them as current CRA performance.

> **Vault research disclaimer (2026-07-23):** The prioritized report *Internal Audit – Tax and Benefits Operations Results Information* was referenced as underway in a **2018** public report, but a **final published report was not located on Canada.ca** during vault research. This **Evaluation – Audit Yield** note is used for **Journey 3** (reporting / results information) in [[00-Start/Public-Audit-Case-Library]].

# Evaluation – Audit Yield

## Official report title

Evaluation – Audit yield

## Publishing branch

[[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]

## Report date

- Final report: **January 2020**
- Canada.ca page details: **2020-02-14** (as verified 2026-07-23)

## Evaluation framing

- Included in the Board-approved **Risk-Based Audit and Evaluation Plan 2019–2022** under *Evaluation Study – CRA’s Management of Closely-Held Business*; evaluation framework approved following the Management Audit and Evaluation Committee meeting in **May 2019**.
- Report scope expanded beyond closely-held businesses to the **full population** of income tax and GST/HST audits for the audit-yield analysis.

## Public background

The CRA annually publishes prior-year audit results, including **fiscal impact** (tax assessed, tax refunds reduced, interest and penalties, and present value of future federal tax assessable from compliance actions). Fiscal impact is reported when an audit **closes** and does **not** account for appeals reversals or uncollected amounts.

The evaluation examines whether CRA can measure **cash recovered**—amounts paid voluntarily or collected through collections—from audit **debit reassessments**, and whether a measure such as **audit yield** (OECD usage: additional tax liabilities **identified and collected** through audit) would improve performance monitoring. The report links this theme to CRA commitments following **Report 7 – Compliance Activities – Canada Revenue Agency** (2018 Fall Reports of the Auditor General).

Audit objectives cited in the report include revenue generation, trust in administration, determining true liability, disincentives to non-compliance, intelligence gathering, and identifying areas needing legislative clarification—not revenue alone.

## Evaluation objective (substantive)

Provide the Commissioner, CRA management, and the [[Board of Management]] with an independent assessment of CRA’s ability to measure the extent to which audit reassessments materialize into **cash recovered**.

## Methodology

**Definition used:** Audit yield as the **rate of recovery on accounts receivable**—actual cash paid or collected directly attributable to audit activities; a **subset** of fiscal impact excluding non-cash items such as **future taxes**.

**Income tax**

- Query approach: **85%** of T2 audit files closed **FY 2015–16** (94% of collectible taxes and penalties).
- Sample approach: **713** debit-reassessment files closed **FY 2016–17**, including all files ≥ **$5 million** (**102** files; **64%** of collectible federal taxes) plus stratified random sample of **611** others; sample segment statistically valid to population at **95% confidence** for the sampled segment.
- Broader appendix reference: **23,146** T1/T2/T3/non-resident files closed **FY 2016–17** with positive assessed tax (methodology appendix).

**GST/HST**

- Population analysis: **20,979** audit files closed **FY 2015–16** with positive GST/HST assessed; refund-only adjustments excluded; matching via Business Number and standardized accounting data (report states matching tested as accurate and reliable).

**Other methods:** Internal interviews; file and document reviews of processes and performance reports.

## Publicly identified organizations

- [[02-Organization/Branches/Compliance Programs Branch|CPB]]
- [[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch]] (results coordination; data as strategic asset)
- [[02-Organization/Branches/Collections and Verification Branch|CVB]]
- Appeals Branch; Assessment, Benefit, and Service Branch (downstream roles, as named in report)
- [[02-Organization/Branches/Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]

## Publicly identified systems or technology concepts

- Audit Information Management System (**AIMS**)
- Integrated Audit Management System (**INTEGRAS**)
- Corporation Tax Processing System (**CORTAX**)
- GST/HST case management and standardized accounting data
- Cross-system matching using audit file number, Business Number, transaction amounts/dates

## Publicly identified data or statistics concepts

- **Fiscal impact** vs **collectible cash** vs **audit yield**
- Debit reassessment, reversal, write-off, under dispute, in collections
- Downstream objections, appeals, and collections workloads
- Fourth-quarter concentration of reassessment **dollar value** (43% income tax; 38% GST/HST of estimated totals in report figures)

## What the published report states

### Finding 4.1 — Recoveries are measurable

As of **July 2019**:

| Program | Cohort | Collectible cash / recovery (report) |
|---------|--------|--------------------------------------|
| Income tax | Debit reassessments closed **FY 2016–17** | **60–64%** of collectible cash recovered; collectible portion **$6.4–6.8B** of **$9.6B** fiscal impact (**67–71%** collectible) |
| GST/HST | Debit reassessments closed **FY 2015–16** | **71%** recovered; **$1.77B** collectible of **$2.60B** fiscal impact (**68%** collectible) |

Table breakdowns include recovered, reversed, written off, under dispute, and in collections categories (income tax shown with ranges). Results expected to change as appeals conclude and collections finish; **not** performance conclusions.

Illustrative cost-effectiveness (Table 3, federal amounts): income tax **4.9:1** (**$3.09B** federal yield / **$633M** direct audit cost); GST/HST **5.9:1** (**$1.25B** / **$211M**).

### Finding 4.2 — Audit yield is relevant for monitoring

Integrated measure supports holistic view across audit, appeals, and collections; examples include cost-effectiveness ratios and downstream workload insight (Q4 reassessment value concentration).

### Finding 4.3 — Automation barriers

GST/HST: **99%** audit case-management files matched reassessments—automation feasible with Business Number.

Income tax: manual matching required; **8%** of T1 INTEGRAS debit files (**FY 2017–18**) lacked matching audit file number in assessing system; **15%** of sampled T2 AIMS files (**FY 2016–17**) unmatched (**22%** of federal tax value). Manual reassessment processing and modernizations cited as contributing factors.

### Recommendations and management response

1. **SIIB** (with CPB and others): adopt and report on an integrated measure periodically calculating cash collected from audits including downstream results (target plan completion **June 30, 2021**, contingent on recommendation 2).
2. **CPB** (with ABS, SIIB, others): changes for efficient automated cross-branch data linking (target **December 31, 2020**); multi-year plan with ITB for data gaps.

CPB and SIIB agreed; work referenced includes GST/HST methodology from prior horizontal evaluation, T1 prototype, and planned T2 prototype with longer timeframe and full data. **T3** redesign noted **out of scope** for audit yield at time of report.

### Conclusion

Audit yield complements fiscal impact with a more fulsome cash outcome story; manual cross-system matching limits repeatable query-based monitoring; expanding to multiple years needed for benchmarks.

## Public limitations

- Single-year cohort snapshots as of **July 2019**; high-dollar appeals may take years.
- Illustrative cost ratios—not prescribed CRA performance targets in the report.
- Income tax matching gaps affect population-level automation confidence.
- Does not replace a dedicated IA on tax and benefits **operations results information** (see disclaimer above).

## Reusable audit and evaluation concepts

- [[Performance Reporting]] · [[Evidence Reliability]]
- [[Population Completeness]] · [[Data Quality]] · [[Missing Data]]
- Evaluation issues: outcomes after audit close; impact on monitoring assumptions (Appendix A)
- Bridges: [[How Data Pipelines Affect Evidence Reliability]] · [[How Public Audit Cases Inform Future Scoping]] · [[How Historical Findings Should Be Used as Precedent]]

## Statistics connections

- Distinct from [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]] and fiscal-year DRF indicators ([[CRA Departmental Results Framework]]).
- [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]] when linking compliance metrics to published aggregates.

## Organizational relationships (labeled)

### Official case-specific relationship

- **Publishing evaluation branch:** [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]
- **Management response / action-plan responsibilities named in report:**
  - [[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch|SIIB]] (with CPB and others) — integrated cash-collected measure
  - [[Compliance Programs Branch|CPB]] (with ABS, SIIB, others) — cross-branch data linking; multi-year plan with [[Information Technology Branch|ITB]] for data gaps
- **Related program context in evaluation framing:** audit results and collections pathways intersect [[Collections and Verification Branch|CVB]] themes (cash recovery), without treating CVB as MAP owner unless the report text assigns it

### Official organizational relationship

- CPB, SIIB, CVB, and ABSB are headquarters **program branches**; ITB is a **corporate branch** on the 2025 Organization baseline

### Derived onboarding interpretation

- Cross-branch data linking is an onboarding example of why performance measures need multiple owners; not an official reporting-line claim

### Historical relationship

- Evaluation final report **January 2020**; analysis snapshot **July 2019**
- Report shorthand **ABS** is recorded as **verification required** relative to current [[Assessment, Benefit, and Service Branch|ABSB]] naming — do not silently equate without report definition

## Related strategic notes

- [[CRA Strategic Priorities]] · [[Compliance Assurance]]

## Related public reports

- [[Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory]]
- [[Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence]]

## Cross-domain interpretation

> **Derived analysis** — not a CRA conclusion.

This vault interprets audit yield as an **integrated outcome metric** requiring explicit definitions, timing, exclusions (non-cash fiscal impact), and cross-system lineage. A performance dashboard cannot be treated as reliable without documented match rates, exception handling, and stated confidence bounds (the **95%** statement applies to the report’s specified income-tax sample segment). See [[How Data Pipelines Affect Evidence Reliability]], [[How Public Audit Cases Inform Future Scoping]], and [[How Historical Findings Should Be Used as Precedent]].

Linking audit files to reassessments to accounting transactions is a **data governance** and **evidence reliability** problem, not only a reporting formula problem—consistent with themes in the BI internal audit case. Unmatched identifiers and snapshot/population limits are interpreted here as [[Missing Data]] and [[Population Completeness]] constraints that narrow how strongly agency-wide recovery conclusions can be stated; see [[How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance]]. Teaching links: [[Data Pipeline]] · [[Data Lineage]] · [[Data Reconciliation]] · [[Management Reporting]] · [[Data Pipeline and Reporting Map]] · [[Stratified Sampling]]. The evaluation period and July 2019 snapshot are historical.

## Questions this case helps a learner explore

1. What question does fiscal impact answer versus cash recovered versus audit yield?
2. When is a population query sufficient, and when is stratified sampling with manual review required?
3. How do unmatched audit file numbers affect interpretability of agency-wide recovery rates?
4. What would “integrated performance monitoring” require across branches named in the report?
5. How should public reporting communicate snapshot estimates without implying current performance?

## Demonstration journey (Journey 3 — reporting)

Start: [[Performance Reporting]] → [[Evidence Reliability]] → [[Population Completeness]] → [[Data Quality]] → [[Missing Data]] → this case → [[Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory]].

## Follow-up evidence in vault

**Current remediation / follow-up status:** unknown in this vault.

This note records the **published** report’s findings, recommendations, and any management action-plan **commitments** (target dates). It does **not** contain a later public follow-up report confirming completion or ongoing operating effectiveness. Do not treat MAP dates as proof of current remediation. See [[Interpreting Historical Public Audit Findings]] and [[Follow-up]].

This note summarizes a publicly released CRA report. It is not an internal working paper, does not contain non-public evidence, and should be read with the original official report.

# Internal Audit – Accounts Receivable National Inventory

> **Historical context:** Findings describe conditions for the audit period **April 1, 2022 to December 31, 2024** (examination January to March 2025; report dated May 14, 2026). Do not assume the same conditions remain unresolved today unless a current official source says so. Separate **what the published report states** from any cross-domain interpretation below.


## What the published report states

**Context.** The Accounts Receivable National Inventory (ARNI) is a Collections and Verification Branch program for tax-debt accounts below $1,000,000 that are automatically risk scored and allocated to officers. It is part of the collections continuum after automated strategies and the debt-management call centre, and before complex collections. In 2024–25, the report states ARNI resolved 171,796 accounts and collected $8.29146 billion in cash.

**Objective and scope.** The objective was assurance that controls were in place and working for effective risk scoring/file allocation and timely, progressive, appropriate collection actions. Scope covered CVB and regional controls over workload, with attention to resource use, inventory management, and account resolution. The period was April 1, 2022 to December 31, 2024; examination was January to March 2025.

**Criteria and methodology.** The audit expected documented strategic goals, aligned procedures and performance expectations; a Decision Support System (DSS) working to documented program needs; and monitoring/performance controls aligned to objectives. Methods were documentation review in CVB and four regions, data analytics using workload-management, DSS, Revenue Enforcement Management and Information Tracking System, and data-mart data, plus interviews with selected staff.

**Findings.** The audit concluded that controls existed for risk scoring/allocation and appropriate collection actions, but processes to monitor that controls worked and address performance issues were limited. It found account churn was not formally defined during examination, and the HQ report did not always reflect movement or program production completely. ARNI Taxpayer Services indicators did not directly contribute to churn, cash collected, or resolution. Roles/processes to assess intended versus actual outcomes of business rules were undocumented, and regional processes affecting allocation/churn had limited controls.

Quality assurance/review tools and guidance were in place. However, the DSS had limited enterprise-level controls for allocating accounts to the right agents and for using system-generated BI; regions used local tools and had been directed not to use DSS data for reporting/decisions. The report also found incomplete performance measures: in 2023–24, 20% of accounts reported as resolved while unassigned/self-resolved had previously been assigned to ARNI, representing about $604.9 million in cash collected; 611 collapsed inventories contained 128,958 accounts. It reported 56% of payment arrangements were suspended at least once, without an apparent HQ/regional mechanism to monitor or address that frequency.

**Recommendations and MAPs.** CVB agreed to define and monitor churn, outputs, officer expectations, and responsive reporting; align ARNI Taxpayer Services objectives/indicators; document governance for business rules; promote DSS use and identify an enterprise solution; and document roles and processes for regional inventory effects. Action-plan targets range from September 2026 through March 2030. The report records a formal churn definition and planning guidelines issued during the audit in May 2025.

**Conclusion.** The historical conclusion separates controls that existed from reported gaps in management controls, decision-support use, and complete/actionable reporting.

**Limitations.** This report does not establish present ARNI performance or the results of future action plans. “Resolved” has a report-specific definition that can include full payment, write-off, or transfer to a higher-complexity workload; it must not be read as cash collected alone.

## Cross-domain interpretation

This vault interprets ARNI as a [[Performance Reporting]] case in which a useful headline metric needs a clear numerator, denominator, business rules, attribution rules, and known exclusions. The report’s examples show why a result can be operationally meaningful yet incomplete for a particular decision—treated here as a [[Missing Data]] and [[Population Completeness]] problem when movement, attribution, or collapsed-inventory views are omitted from the measure used for the decision. See [[How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance]]. Historical findings are not a claim about current ARNI completeness.

This vault also interprets the DSS finding through [[Business Intelligence]], [[Data Governance]], and [[Evidence Reliability]]. Risk scoring, allocation, local workarounds, and reported outcomes form a feedback loop: a decision-support system needs documented ownership, validation, monitoring of intended versus actual results, and usable reporting before its data can support enterprise learning.

## Questions this case helps a learner explore

- How would you define account churn so it remains comparable across regions and time?
- What reconciliation would show where production credit changes when an account moves?
- Which indicators distinguish cash collection, resolution, inventory movement, and effort on complex referrals?
- How could controls test whether risk scoring and allocation support the intended operational outcomes?
- What information must be complete before a dashboard is decision-useful?

## Reusable concepts and connections

- [[Performance Reporting]] — definitions, attribution, timeliness, and actionable measures.
- [[Business Intelligence]] and [[Data Governance]] — DSS data ownership, permitted use, and feedback.
- [[Data Quality]], [[Missing Data]], and [[Evidence Reliability]] — completeness of movement, payment, and allocation records.
- [[Population Completeness]] — include assigned/unassigned, transferred, and collapsed inventory views where relevant.
- Bridges: [[How Data Quality Affects Management Reporting]] · [[How Data Pipelines Affect Evidence Reliability]] · [[How Public Audit Cases Inform Future Scoping]] · [[How Historical Findings Should Be Used as Precedent]]

## Software, statistics, and organizational connections

**Software:** the Decision Support System is reported as an authorized system for distribution, inventory, and business rules; it was not intended by this report to be an unqualified reporting source. **Statistics:** the reported counts, cash, inventories, and suspended arrangements illustrate attribution and completeness issues.

## Organizational relationships (labeled)

### Official case-specific relationship

- **Publishing assurance branch:** [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]
- **Office of primary interest / program owner named in report:** [[Collections and Verification Branch|CVB]] (ARNI program)
- **Management response / MAP owner:** [[Collections and Verification Branch|CVB]] agreed to recommendations and action plans
- **Scope / examined areas:** CVB and regional controls across four regions ([[Atlantic Region]], [[Quebec Region]], [[Ontario Region]], [[Western Region]])

### Official organizational relationship

- CVB is a headquarters **program branch** ([[CRA-Program-Branches]]); regions deliver programs via field offices ([[CRA-Regions]])

### Derived onboarding interpretation

- Interdependence of HQ and regional inventory monitoring is explained for onboarding; it is **not** an official org-chart reporting line beyond what the report states

### Historical relationship

- Report findings cover April 2022–December 2024; do not treat as current ARNI performance

## Follow-up evidence in vault

**Current remediation / follow-up status:** unknown in this vault.

This note records the **published** report’s findings, recommendations, and any management action-plan **commitments** (target dates). It does **not** contain a later public follow-up report confirming completion or ongoing operating effectiveness. Do not treat MAP dates as proof of current remediation. See [[Interpreting Historical Public Audit Findings]] and [[Follow-up]].

This note summarizes a publicly released CRA report. It is not an internal working paper, does not contain non-public evidence, and should be read with the original official report.

# Internal Audit – Charities Audit Process

> **Historical context:** Findings describe conditions for the audit period **April 1, 2020 to March 31, 2023** (examination June 2023 to January 2024; report dated January 2025 in vault frontmatter). Do not assume the same conditions remain unresolved today unless a current official source says so. Separate **what the published report states** from any cross-domain interpretation below.


## What the published report states

**Context.** The Charities Directorate (CD) within the Legislative Policy and Regulatory Affairs Branch (LPRAB) promotes compliance with legislation relating to charities through education and enforcement. Its Compliance Division manages general charities compliance, while the Review and Analysis Division (RAD) manages a program focused on terrorism-abuse and non-compliance risks. The report states that approximately 86,000 Canadian charities were federally registered and that the two divisions completed 545 audits from 2020–21 through 2022–23: 541 by Compliance and 4 by RAD.

**Objective and scope.** The audit sought assurance that key audit processes were in place and followed for the impartial conduct of CD audits. Scope included planning and information gathering, risk assessment, workload identification, audit methodologies, and monitoring/oversight. It excluded a broader effectiveness review, detailed review of how audits were conducted, and broader AML-ATF or national-security activities outside RAD. The period was April 1, 2020 to March 31, 2023; examination was June 2023 to January 2024.

**Criteria and methodology.** Criteria covered: (1) established and communicated processes, documented/reviewed plans and risk approaches, and controls over information, leads, BI, and potential audit-file assessment/approval; and (2) monitoring for impartiality plus oversight mechanisms. Methods included document review; interviews and walkthroughs at headquarters and regional offices; review of control outcomes and supporting documentation, including taxpayer and classified information; application-data analysis for statistics and indicators; review of reporting; and meetings coordinated with Security Branch and NSIRA.

**Findings.** Workflows, plans, and much oversight were established, but improvements were needed to demonstrate impartiality and consistency. RAD risk indicators were last updated and approved in December 2016, without a formal periodic-review requirement. The report found gaps in formal information-gathering processes, review checkpoints, standards, terminology, documentation of risk levels and treatments, and documented approvals. It noted manual work across systems, limited/incomplete data dispersed across sources, and limited ability to report on impartiality across the population. File reviews covered 21 risk-assessed cases and 18 completed audits; documented reviews and approvals were not always complete. Monitoring largely used operational metrics and did not explicitly cover impartiality and consistent treatment across cases.

**Recommendations and MAPs.** LPRAB was recommended to require periodic review/approval of RAD risk indicators; formalize roles, procedures, quality review, detailed criteria/tools, and decision documentation; improve information systems/BI strategy/reporting; and expand data gathering and monitoring/reporting for impartiality. LPRAB agreed. Action plans included documented interdepartmental/external-review outcomes and formal risk-indicator review (March 2026); roles, job aids, checkpoints, RAD procedures, and risk recording (targets March 2025 to March 2026); modernization/BI options and consultations (to March 2026); and quality-assurance and monitoring improvements (to September 2025).

**Conclusion.** The report concluded that workflows were communicated and planning/oversight generally existed, but the manually intensive, judgment-dependent process required stronger controls to demonstrate impartial and consistent decisions.

**Limitations.** This report’s findings concern the reviewed period and scope. It contains redacted material, and this note does not summarize classified or taxpayer information.

> Public source limitation: Certain information was not disclosed in the published report. This vault does not attempt to reconstruct it.

## Cross-domain interpretation

This vault interprets the report as an operational [[Data Quality]] and [[Evidence Reliability]] case: impartiality is supported not only by a decision’s rationale, but by structured inputs, consistent terminology, retained approvals, traceable review evidence, and population-level monitoring. Manual transfers across systems increase the need for explicit reconciliation and quality controls; this is not a claim that automation alone assures fairness.

This vault interprets the report’s limited/incomplete data dispersed across sources, and limited population-level impartiality reporting, as a [[Missing Data]] and [[Population Completeness]] concern: a performance view based only on open/closed files and outcomes may not show whether comparable cases received comparable treatments. The reported model implemented in April 2024 and planned actions are management responses, not evidence that historical gaps were already resolved. See [[How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance]].

## Questions this case helps a learner explore

- What fields, review evidence, and approvals make a risk-based selection decision reproducible?
- How would you test the completeness and consistency of a population of audit treatments?
- Which risks can algorithmic screening reduce, and which require governance over data, thresholds, and review?
- How should quality assurance be designed to assess impartiality without accessing unnecessary sensitive information?
- How can operational metrics be complemented by measures of consistency and decision quality?

## Reusable concepts and connections

- [[Business Intelligence]], [[Data Governance]], and [[Data Quality]] — inputs, definitions, and decision support.
- [[Missing Data]] · [[Population Completeness]] — whether reporting covers cases and treatments needed for a conclusion.
- [[Evidence Reliability]] — documented decisions, retained work, and review trails.
- [[Performance Reporting]] — operational counts alone may not evidence impartiality.
- [[Three Lines Model]] — a general lens for operational controls, monitoring, and assurance.
- Bridges: [[How Data Quality Affects Management Reporting]] · [[How Statistical Bias Can Mislead an Audit]] · [[How Historical Findings Should Be Used as Precedent]]

## Software, statistics, and organizational connections

**Software:** the report describes separate systems, networks, and spreadsheets supporting manual work; it does not prescribe a particular replacement. **Statistics:** file reviews of 21 risk-assessed cases and 18 completed audits informed findings but are not a population estimate.

## Organizational relationships (labeled)

### Official case-specific relationship

- **Publishing assurance branch:** [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]
- **Office of primary interest / responsible program area:** Charities Directorate within [[Legislative Policy and Regulatory Affairs Branch|LPRAB]]
- **Management response / MAP owner:** [[Legislative Policy and Regulatory Affairs Branch|LPRAB]] agreed to recommendations and action plans
- **Methodology coordination named in report:** [[02-Organization/Branches/Security Branch]]; regional offices / tax services offices

### Official organizational relationship

- LPRAB is a headquarters **program branch** on the 2025 Organization baseline ([[CRA-Program-Branches]])
- Regions deliver via field offices including Tax Services Offices ([[CRA-Regions]])

### Derived onboarding interpretation

- Security Branch coordination does **not** by itself establish a reporting line to LPRAB; it is case methodology context only

### Historical relationship

- None required beyond the report’s own audit period (2020–21 to 2022–23)

## Follow-up evidence in vault

**Current remediation / follow-up status:** unknown in this vault.

It does **not** contain a later public follow-up report confirming completion or ongoing operating effectiveness. Do not treat MAP dates as proof of current remediation. This note summarizes a publicly released CRA report. It is not an internal working paper, does not contain non-public evidence, and should be read with the original official report.

# Internal Audit – Enterprise Fraud Management System

> **Historical context:** Findings describe conditions for the audit period **April 1, 2021 to March 31, 2024** (with pertinent activities since 2017; examination July to December 2024; report dated January 23, 2026). Do not assume the same conditions remain unresolved today unless a current official source says so. Do not reconstruct protected/redacted detail. Separate **what the published report states** from any cross-domain interpretation below.


## What the published report states

**Context.** CRA implemented the Enterprise Fraud Management System (EFMS) in 2017 to reduce risks of unauthorized employee access to taxpayer information. The system records employee transactions and uses business rules to identify questionable activity in real time. The Security Branch’s Internal Fraud Management Solutions (IFMS) Section maintains/enhances EFMS and supports system developers; Internal Affairs reviews alerts. ITB’s Enterprise Fraud Management Services Section maintains EFMS. The report states that EFMS generated more than 17,000 alerts since implementation, including 2,334 in 2022–23 and 1,850 in 2023–24.

**Objective and scope.** The audit sought assurance that EFMS was working as intended by recording, managing, monitoring, and reporting user activities in accordance with CRA policy instruments. It covered capture of audit-trail records through receipt of alerts, not processes after Internal Affairs screening, including investigations and discipline. The period was April 1, 2021 to March 31, 2024, with pertinent activities since 2017; examination was July to December 2024.

**Criteria and methodology.** Criteria concerned application onboarding, review/modification of detection models (business rules), timely alert receipt, and accurate/relevant performance information. The published methodology says it reviewed documentation from Security Branch and ITB to verify policies, procedures, and practices.

**Findings.** The audit concluded EFMS was working as intended, with improvement opportunities. Application onboarding had procedures but lacked a formal risk-assessment framework and formal time-estimation procedures. Business-rule changes were ad hoc across owners; oversight was inconsistent, detailed change history was not centrally maintained, and some rules had not been reviewed or modified even when they generated many false-positive alerts. Record loading had a process and expected-record matching, but was not always timely and controlled. A quarterly dashboard reported six indicators, but the audit identified additional indicators—such as alert resolution by rule and timing from incident to incident/alert creation—that could better inform management.

**Recommendations and MAPs.** Security Branch agreed to document formal onboarding risk assessments with effort considerations; monitor and track business-rule changes; formalize record re-ingestion with expected timeframes and user communications, jointly with ITB; and develop KPIs for efficiency/effectiveness. Action plans included a standardized rule-note field, review of high false-positive rules, centralized re-ingestion material, and improved alert-resolution definitions/data. Targets were May 2026.

**Conclusion.** The public conclusion is positive on the system working as intended while specifically identifying governance, timeliness/control, and performance-measure improvements.

**Limitations.** The report excludes the investigation and discipline stages and contains security-related redactions. It does not disclose system configuration, protected rule details, or a complete assessment of internal-fraud risk.

> Public source limitation: Certain information was not disclosed in the published report. This vault does not attempt to reconstruct it.

## Cross-domain interpretation

This vault interprets the case as a [[Cybersecurity]] monitoring and [[Data Governance]] case. An alerting system’s technical operation, its rule-change governance, data timeliness, and decision-useful metrics each form separate control objectives. A low-level rule change may affect alert volume, false positives, workload, detection coverage, and reporting; centralized, traceable change evidence supports [[Evidence Reliability]] without exposing protected rule logic.

This vault interprets the loading/re-ingestion finding through [[Defence in Depth]]: detection depends on data reaching the monitoring layer in a controlled and timely way, while response depends on the downstream process that was outside scope. This does not imply that the report found a particular exposure or failure. Completeness of transfers into the monitoring layer is also a [[Missing Data]] and [[Data Quality]] concern for evidence of timely detection; see [[How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance]]. Historical findings and public redactions are not a current-state fraud-risk assessment.

## Questions this case helps a learner explore

- What risk factors and effort estimates should an application-onboarding framework record?
- What minimum evidence should accompany a detection-rule change?
- Which KPIs distinguish alert volume from detection quality, timeliness, and operational effectiveness?
- How can a re-ingestion process validate completeness and communicate its potential impact?
- Where should a system audit’s boundary be drawn between monitoring, investigation, and discipline?

## Reusable concepts and connections

- [[Cybersecurity]] and [[Defence in Depth]] — audit trails, detection, and timely monitoring.
- [[Unauthorized Access]] · [[Audit Logging]] · [[Monitoring and Alerting]] — detective monitoring themes (not an entitlement-provisioning audit).
- [[Automated Business Rules]] · [[Change Management]] · [[False Positives]] — rule governance and outcome quality.
- [[Data Governance]] — ownership, formal changes, and standardized definitions.
- [[Evidence Reliability]], [[Data Quality]], [[Missing Data]], [[Rejected Records]] — record completeness, timeliness, and traceable rule history.
- [[System-Generated Evidence]] — alert counts/dashboards alone may be insufficient.
- [[Performance Reporting]] — indicators must support decisions, not merely describe volume.
- [[Three Lines Model]] — a general framework for separating system operation, oversight, and assurance.
- Maps: [[Logging and Monitoring Map]] · [[Automated Controls Map]]
- Bridges: [[How Automated Controls Are Audited]] · [[How Logging Supports Audit Evidence]] · [[How Software Changes Create Compliance Risk]] · [[How Historical Findings Should Be Used as Precedent]]

## Software, statistics, and organizational connections

**Software:** EFMS combines audit-trail ingestion, rule-based alerting, and re-ingestion processes; protected configuration details are not summarized. **Statistics:** alert counts, timing intervals, and false-positive patterns are candidate operational measures, not sufficient evidence by themselves.

## Organizational relationships (labeled)

### Official case-specific relationship

- **Publishing assurance branch:** [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]
- **Primary management respondent / MAP owner:** [[02-Organization/Branches/Security Branch]] (IFMS Section maintains/enhances EFMS; agreed to action plans)
- **Named co-responsible for selected actions:** [[Information Technology Branch|ITB]] (Enterprise Fraud Management Services Section maintains EFMS; jointly named for re-ingestion formalization)
- **Other named operational role in report:** Internal Affairs reviews alerts (unit named in report; not expanded into an unsupported branch ownership claim here)

### Official organizational relationship

- Security Branch and ITB are headquarters **corporate branches** ([[CRA-Corporate-Branches]])

### Derived onboarding interpretation

- Shared EFMS maintenance is a case-stated collaboration; it does **not** by itself prove a reporting line between Security Branch and ITB

### Historical relationship

- EFMS implemented 2017; audit period April 2021–March 2024 (with pertinent activities since 2017)

## Follow-up evidence in vault

**Current remediation / follow-up status:** unknown in this vault.

This note records the **published** report’s findings, recommendations, and any management action-plan **commitments** (target dates). It does **not** contain a later public follow-up report confirming completion or ongoing operating effectiveness. Do not treat MAP dates as proof of current remediation. See [[Interpreting Historical Public Audit Findings]] and [[Follow-up]].

> This note summarizes a publicly released CRA report. It is not an internal working paper, does not contain non-public evidence, and should be read with the original official report.

> **Historical context:** Findings describe conditions identified for the audit period **1 April 2020 to 31 March 2023**. Do not assume the same conditions remain unresolved today unless a current official source says so.

# Internal Audit — Oversight, Use, and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence

## Official report title

Internal Audit – Oversight, Use, and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence

## Publishing branch

[[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]

## Report date

- Final report presented to the Audit Committee: **18 June 2024**
- Canada.ca page details date: **2024-10-15** (as verified 2026-07-23)

## Audit period

- Coverage: **1 April 2020 – 31 March 2023**
- Examination phase: **June 2023 – November 2023**
- Included in the 2022–2023 Risk-Based Assurance and Advisory Plan (Mid-Year Update), approved by the Board of Management on **30 March 2022**
- Assignment Planning Memorandum approved by the Commissioner on **11 September 2023**

## Public background

The published report states that the CRA creates and collects taxpayer information and holds millions of taxpayer data records used for purposes including developing [[Business Intelligence]] to support compliance, collections, and verification.

The report defines business intelligence as information derived from available data that provides knowledge and insights to support decision-making and program administration. BI may include reporting, [[Analytics]], and [[Research]].

[[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch|SIIB]] has held responsibility for BI activities since 2011, with service delivery by [[Information Technology Branch|ITB]]. The [[Chief Data Officer]] is also the Assistant Commissioner of SIIB. The report notes decentralized BI capacity across branches and regions as demand grew after 2011.

In 2020 the CRA introduced the [[Information and Data Strategy]], with four pillars: governance, people and culture, environment and infrastructure, and supporting innovation and transformation.

## Importance

The report states the audit is important because CRA BI capacity expanded rapidly and the CRA committed to optimizing data use, facilitating sharing and collaboration, increasing usability and reusability, and supporting [[Evidence-Based Decision-Making]].

## Audit objective

Provide the Commissioner, CRA management, and the [[Board of Management]] with assurance that business intelligence is being overseen and used, and continuously improved, to support compliance, collections, and verification programs.

## Scope

**In scope:** governance structures, uses, and continuous improvement of business intelligence.

**Out of scope (as stated):** examination of data security; human resource challenges; applications, tools, and infrastructure and their lifecycle used to develop BI.

## Audit criteria

Line of enquiry (Appendix A): a management control framework is in place for BI to support compliance, collections, and verification, including documented framework elements (data governance; responsible business areas; enterprise and branch/regional strategies; roles/responsibilities/accountability; approval levels; monitoring and reporting; leadership), clarity of roles for senior management/stakeholders, an oversight process for enterprise-view tool acquisition aligned with the Information and Data Strategy, and a structure fostering continuous improvement.

## Methodology

Documented methodology included:

- Document review of roles, strategies, policies, terms of reference, and IT architecture governance records
- Process/methodology review of selected CPB and CVB teams using BI
- Interviews with stakeholders in SIIB, ITB, CVB, CPB, DTPB, and BI Quality Assurance in Western, Ontario, Quebec, and Atlantic regions
- Observation of governance committee and working-group meetings

Conducted in accordance with the International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing.

## Publicly identified organizations

- [[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch]]
- [[02-Organization/Branches/Information Technology Branch|ITB]]
- [[02-Organization/Branches/Collections and Verification Branch|CVB]]
- [[02-Organization/Branches/Compliance Programs Branch|CPB]]
- [[02-Organization/Branches/Digital Transformation Program Branch|DTPB]]
- Business Intelligence and Quality Assurance (Western, Ontario, Quebec, Atlantic regions)
- Business Intelligence Director General Steering Committee (BIDGSC), co-chaired by SIIB and ITB

## Publicly identified business processes

- BI governance and oversight
- Tool [[Tool Acquisition|acquisition]] and [[Tool Deployment|deployment]]
- Workload development supported by BI
- Working groups for collaboration and continuous improvement
- Horizontal coordination of BI efforts

## Publicly identified systems or technology concepts

- Business intelligence tools and self-service systems (named only at concept level in the public report)
- Research and artificial intelligence repositories (mentioned; the report states no established CRA-wide BI repository was observed)

## Publicly identified data or statistics concepts

- [[Structured Data]] and [[Unstructured Information]] as information assets
- [[Data Governance]]
- Risk algorithms and [[Artificial Intelligence]] (as forms of analytics produced by BI developers, per glossary)
- Decentralized BI development and horizontal reuse

## What the published report states

### Overall conclusion

Important components of the BI framework are in place; some improvements are needed to strengthen it.

### Published findings (paraphrased)

1. **Governance framework:** Documented governance exists for management of data and acquisition of tools. Actions required: establish CRA-wide objectives for BI; clarify [[Roles and Responsibilities]]; determine a common definition of BI.
2. **Strategy:** The BI strategy evolved toward data governance and tool acquisition but was missing strategies to leverage and coordinate BI horizontally.
3. **Working groups / collaboration:** Working groups foster continuous improvement, but limited horizontal collaborations were observed; developers often worked in silos; many workload teams collaborated only within program/branch groups.
4. **Continuous improvement:** No CRA-wide expectations for developing BI; inconsistent continuous improvement processes; instances where potentially outdated BI was not reviewed and updated for multiple years.
5. **Tool deployment:** An oversight body/process exists for enterprise view when acquiring tools, but no formal process supported effective and timely deployment to BI teams Agency-wide.

### Published recommendations

SIIB, in collaboration with ITB and other stakeholders, should strengthen the BI governance framework by:

1. Establishing CRA-wide BI objectives, clear roles and responsibilities, and a common BI definition
2. Developing a strategy to coordinate, leverage, and monitor BI efforts horizontally so BI meets program decision-making needs and supports CRA strategic priorities
3. Establishing expectations for developing BI, including continuous improvement requirements
4. Developing an effective deployment process for timely delivery of BI tools

### Published management responses and action-plan dates

SIIB agrees; AERB judged action plans reasonable. Public action-plan commitments include (paraphrased):

- **By March 2025:** AC-level collaboration to establish enterprise-wide BI objectives/direction; document definitions, roles/responsibilities, links to AI Enablement Plan and Information and Data Strategy
- **By June 2025:** Enhance/coordinate/leverage/monitor BI horizontally (including cloud capability strategy work with ITB)
- **By June 2025:** Scan BI areas and peer international organizations; plan to strengthen BI community of practice
- **By December 2024:** Review last BI tool deployment and identify steps for a new formal process

### Conclusion (report)

Restates that important framework components exist and that improvements are needed in objectives/roles/definition, horizontal strategy, collaboration, continuous improvement expectations, and tool deployment process.

## Public limitations or redactions

No major ATIP-style redaction blocks were noted in the HTML report as verified 2026-07-23. Out-of-scope items (security, HR, tool/infrastructure lifecycle) are intentionally not covered.

## Reusable audit concepts

- [[Audit Objective]] · [[Scope]] · [[Criteria]] · [[Methodology]]
- [[Finding]] · [[Recommendation]] · [[Management Response]] · [[Management Action Plan]]
- [[Business Intelligence Governance]] · [[Horizontal Collaboration]] · [[Continuous Improvement]]
- Bridges: [[How Organizational Ownership Affects System Accountability]] · [[How Public Audit Cases Inform Future Scoping]] · [[How Historical Findings Should Be Used as Precedent]]

## Software connections

- [[Business Intelligence Tools]] · [[Tool Acquisition]] · [[Tool Deployment]]
- [[Artificial Intelligence]] · [[Structured Data]] · [[Unstructured Information]]

## Statistics connections

- Aggregate data used to produce BI is distinct from published statistical products such as [[Individual Income Tax Return Statistics]]
- [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]] remains relevant when BI or performance stories rely on incomplete or suppressed data; see [[Missing Data]] (and distinguish accidental gaps from [[Data Suppression]])

## Organizational relationships (labeled)

### Official case-specific relationship

- **Publishing assurance branch:** [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]] (also judged action plans reasonable)
- **Primary BI responsibility / MAP lead named in report:** [[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch|SIIB]] (BI since 2011; SIIB agrees to recommendations)
- **Service delivery partner named in report:** [[Information Technology Branch|ITB]] (BI service delivery; BIDGSC co-chair with SIIB; named in action-plan collaboration)
- **Teams / stakeholders examined or interviewed:** [[Compliance Programs Branch|CPB]], [[Collections and Verification Branch|CVB]], [[Digital Transformation Program Branch|DTPB]], and BI Quality Assurance in Western, Ontario, Quebec, and Atlantic regions
- **Chief Data Officer:** Assistant Commissioner of SIIB ([[Chief Data Officer]])

### Official organizational relationship

- SIIB is a **program branch**; ITB and DTPB are **corporate branches**; CPB and CVB are **program branches** ([[CRA-Program-Branches]], [[CRA-Corporate-Branches]])
- Regions deliver programs via field offices ([[CRA-Regions]])

### Derived onboarding interpretation

- Multi-branch BI work illustrates why audits span owners without implying a single reporting hierarchy among SIIB/ITB/CPB/CVB/DTPB

### Historical relationship

- Audit period 1 April 2020 – 31 March 2023; BI responsibility statement “since 2011” is historical context from the report

## Related strategic notes

- [[CRA Strategic Priorities]]

## Related public reports

- [[Internal Audit - Specific Cyber Security Controls]]
- [[Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System]]
- [[Evaluation - Audit Yield]]

## Cross-domain interpretation

> This vault interprets the issue as relevant to knowledge fragmentation and reuse. This is **derived analysis**, not a CRA conclusion.

The published report states that absence of a CRA-wide BI repository elevates duplication risk and limits horizontal leverage. This vault interprets that pattern as conceptually related to why a governed public knowledge corpus (and, later, retrieval with source filters) can reduce duplicated analytical effort—**without claiming** the audit recommended Obsidian, RAG, or this MVP.

Separately, when BI or performance narratives rely on incomplete extracts or suppressed aggregates, this vault links the assurance limit to [[Missing Data]] and [[How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance]]—without treating suppression as accidental data loss, and without claiming current BI data quality from this historical report.

A possible cross-domain relationship is:

```text
[[Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence]]
→ examines
[[Business Intelligence Governance]]
→ depends on
[[Roles and Responsibilities]]

[[Business Intelligence]]
→ uses
[[Structured Data]]
and
[[Unstructured Information]]

[[Continuous Improvement]]
→ mitigates
[[Outdated Analytics]]

[[Horizontal Collaboration]]
→ reduces
[[Duplicate Analytical Work]]
```

See also: [[How the CRA Business Intelligence Audit Supports the Knowledge-Vault Concept]]

## Questions this case helps a learner explore

1. How should an auditor distinguish a governance finding from a technical-tool finding?
2. What evidence would show that continuous improvement is operating, not just informal peer review?
3. How do unclear definitions of “business intelligence” affect scope and criteria?
4. What is the difference between tool acquisition oversight and tool deployment control?
5. How should action-plan dates be tracked without assuming current unresolved status?

## Demonstration journey

Start: [[Business Intelligence]] → [[Data Governance]] → [[Horizontal Collaboration]] → [[Continuous Improvement]] → [[Duplicate Analytical Work]] → this case.

**Current remediation / follow-up status:** unknown in this vault.

This note records the **published** report’s findings, recommendations, and any management action-plan **commitments** (target dates). It does **not** contain a later public follow-up report confirming completion or ongoing operating effectiveness. Do not treat MAP dates as proof of current remediation. See [[Interpreting Historical Public Audit Findings]] and [[Follow-up]].

08-Cases/Internal Audit - Specific Cyber.body:
This note summarizes a publicly released CRA report. It is not an internal working paper, does not contain non-public evidence, and should be read with the original official report.

# Internal Audit – Specific Cyber Security Controls

> **Historical context:** Findings and recommendations describe conditions for the audited period **December 1, 2021 to August 31, 2022** (examination May to August 2022; report dated March 2023). Do not assume the same conditions remain unresolved today unless a current official source says so. Protected finding detail must not be reconstructed. Separate **what the published report states** from any cross-domain interpretation below.


## What the published report states

**Report context.** This Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch report is dated March 2023. For April 1, 2021 to March 31, 2022, the report stated that the CRA administered more than $586.3 billion in revenues and pension contributions; 91% of individual and 94% of corporate returns were filed digitally, and 89% of tax services were online. Budget 2021 was stated to propose $332 million over five years and $51.2 million ongoing for cyber security.

**Objective, scope, and period.** The objective was assurance that controls were in place and working to safeguard CRA IT from digital attack. The audited period was December 1, 2021 to August 31, 2022; examination occurred from May to August 2022. The report covered a subset of higher-risk controls, not the entire cyber-security posture.

**Findings and recommendations.** The published report identified areas needing improvement, but the content is protected. It recommended that the Security Branch establish a second line of defence for cyber security to evaluate and monitor controls, and update corporate policy instruments to align with the Treasury Board Policy on Service and Digital. Other recommendations are protected.

**Management response and organizational context.** The Security Branch agreed. The report records the shared Security Branch/AERB opinion that the audit did not reveal vulnerabilities leaving the CRA open to immediate attack, while describing the audit as valuable in identifying symptoms of a larger cyber-governance gap. It states that the Security Branch was formed and that the Agency Security Officer’s role increased as of April 2022. It identifies first-line responsibility in CISD, a planned GRC capability as second line by March 2024, and AERB as third line.

**Conclusion.** The public report supplies assurance language and selected governance improvements, but does not disclose the protected finding details or the full recommendation set.

**Limitations.** This is a historical, deliberately limited audit of selected controls. It neither assesses the complete cyber posture nor supports claims about the CRA’s current vulnerabilities or control effectiveness.

> Public source limitation: Certain information was not disclosed in the published report. This vault does not attempt to reconstruct it.

## Cross-domain interpretation

This vault interprets the published organizational description through [[Defence in Depth]] and the [[Three Lines Model]]. The distinction matters: operational cyber teams can own and operate controls; an independent second-line function can set expectations, challenge assessments, and monitor control effectiveness; internal audit can provide third-line assurance. This is an interpretive learning lens, not a reconstruction of protected findings.

This vault further interprets alignment with the Treasury Board policy as a governance question connecting [[Cybersecurity]], policy instruments, risk ownership, and [[Evidence Reliability]]. A learner can ask what evidence each line needs to demonstrate that a control is designed, operating, monitored, and escalated—without inferring particular technical controls.

## Questions this case helps a learner explore

- Why might a cyber program need second-line monitoring distinct from the team operating controls?
- How can a subset-of-controls audit provide assurance without representing a complete posture assessment?
- What distinguishes a control owner’s evidence from second-line monitoring and third-line assurance?
- How does [[Defence in Depth]] combine governance, people, process, and technology controls?
- What claims are unsafe to make when a published report contains protected content?

## Reusable concepts and connections

- [[Cybersecurity]] — safeguarding IT and information against digital attack.
- [[Defence in Depth]] — layered prevention, detection, response, and recovery.
- [[Three Lines Model]] — first-line CISD, planned second-line GRC capacity, and third-line AERB as described in the report.
- [[Data Governance]] — policy, accountability, and evidence structures complement technical safeguards.
- [[Evidence Reliability]] — report redactions constrain what can be concluded.
- NIST Cybersecurity Framework: IDENTIFY, PROTECT, DETECT, RESPOND, and RECOVER, cited in the report context.

## Software, statistics, and organizational connections

**Software:** the report concerns a selected subset of controls over CRA IT, not a disclosed technical control inventory. **Statistics:** the published digital-service figures establish operating context only; they are not cyber-control performance measures.

## Organizational relationships (labeled)

### Official case-specific relationship

- **Publishing assurance branch / third line (as described in report):** [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]
- **Management response owner:** [[02-Organization/Branches/Security Branch]] agreed
- **Three Lines description in report:** CISD as first line; planned GRC capability as second line; AERB as third line ([[Three Lines Model]])
- **Historical formation fact in report:** Security Branch formed and Agency Security Officer role increased as of April 2022

### Official organizational relationship

- Security Branch is a headquarters **corporate branch** ([[CRA-Corporate-Branches]])

### Derived onboarding interpretation

- Enterprise IT/cyber themes often involve [[Information Technology Branch|ITB]] in learning paths; this case’s protected content does **not** support inventing ITB MAP ownership here

### Historical relationship

- Report dated March 2023; Security Branch formation context as of April 2022 per report

## Follow-up evidence in vault

**Current remediation / follow-up status:** unknown in this vault.

This note records the **published** report’s findings, recommendations, and any management action-plan **commitments** (target dates). It does **not** contain a later public follow-up report confirming completion or ongoing operating effectiveness. Do not treat MAP dates as proof of current remediation. See [[Interpreting Historical Public Audit Findings]] and [[Follow-up]].

## Sources

- [Internal Audit – Specific Cyber Security Controls (official CRA report)](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/programs/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/internal-audit-program-evaluation/internal-audit-program-evaluation-reports-2023/internal-audit-specific-cyber-security-controls.html) — accessed 2026-07-23.

# Public CRA audit and evaluation case studies

This folder contains learning notes that summarize **publicly released** CRA internal audit and evaluation reports. Each case separates **what the published report states** from this vault’s clearly labelled **cross-domain interpretation**. Historical findings are not statements about current CRA conditions unless a newer official source says so. See [[Interpreting Historical Public Audit Findings]]. Each case should include a **Follow-up evidence in vault** section stating current remediation status is unknown unless a follow-up source is linked.

Master index with demo journeys: [[00-Start/Public-Audit-Case-Library]].

## Case index

| # | Case note | Report type | Primary themes |
|---|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| 1 | [[Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence]] | Internal audit (2024) | BI governance, horizontal coordination, tool deployment, continuous improvement |
| 2 | [[Internal Audit - Specific Cyber Security Controls]] | Internal audit (2023) | Subset cyber controls, second line, policy alignment; protected findings |
| 3 | [[Internal Audit - Charities Audit Process]] | Internal audit (2025) | Risk-based process, impartiality, documentation, monitoring |
| 4 | [[Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory]] | Internal audit (2026) | Collections inventory, risk scoring, DSS/BI use, performance measures |
| 5 | [[Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System]] | Internal audit (2026) | EFMS rules, audit trails, re-ingestion, KPIs |
| 6 | [[Evaluation - Audit Yield]] | Evaluation (2020) | Fiscal impact vs cash recovery, cross-system matching, snapshot limits |

## Journey 1 — Governance, technology, and control design

Start with [[Internal Audit - Oversight Use and Continuous Improvement of Business Intelligence]] to distinguish data/tool governance from the governance of BI products and their lifecycle. Continue to [[Internal Audit - Specific Cyber Security Controls]] and [[Internal Audit - Enterprise Fraud Management System]] for policy alignment, monitoring technology, and report redaction limits.

Useful concepts: [[Business Intelligence]], [[Data Governance]], [[Cybersecurity]], [[Defence in Depth]], [[Three Lines Model]], [[Evidence Reliability]].

## Journey 2 — Operational decisions and fairness

Read [[Internal Audit - Charities Audit Process]] for information gathering, risk assessment, documented approvals, and monitoring supporting consistent decisions. Then [[Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory]] for national collections/inventory, risk scoring, local practices, and management information.

Useful concepts: [[Population Completeness]], [[Missing Data]], [[Data Quality]], [[Evidence Reliability]], [[Performance Reporting]], [[Business Intelligence]].

## Journey 3 — Reporting, statistics, and outcomes

Begin with [[Evaluation - Audit Yield]] (public reporting/results-information demo). It contrasts fiscal impact and cash-recovery outcomes, documents population and sample methods, and explains cross-system matching barriers. Follow with [[Internal Audit - Accounts Receivable National Inventory]] for metric definition, attribution, timeliness, and inventory movement.

**Disclaimer (vault research 2026-07-23):** *Internal Audit – Tax and Benefits Operations Results Information* was referenced as underway in **2018** public material; a **final published report was not located on Canada.ca**. Journey 3 uses Evaluation – Audit Yield instead.

Useful concepts: [[Performance Reporting]], [[Population Completeness]], [[Missing Data]], [[Data Quality]], [[Evidence Reliability]], [[Business Intelligence]], [[Data Governance]], [[How Statistical Limitations Affect Audit Conclusions]], [[How Missing Data Limits Audit Assurance]].

## Source practice

Open each note’s official Canada.ca URL (see [[99-Sources/CRA-Public-Source-Register]] and matching `SRC-*` source notes) before relying on a claim. Treat redacted material and out-of-scope subjects as unknown. Treat management action plans as intended responses, not evidence of completion.

# Audit Committee

The Audit Committee is a committee of the CRA **Board of Management**. A **public charter** is published on Canada.ca.

## Public mandate or responsibility

From the source facts available for this vault note (high-level governance context, not full charter text):

- The **Board** oversees CRA organization and management and supports world-class tax and benefit administration ([[Board of Management]]).
- Board-level governance connects to **internal audit and program evaluation (IA/PE)** planning and reporting in the public governance story of the agency; [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]] and the IA landing page describe IA/PE as supporting strategic goals with independent assurance and public posting of results. See [[CRA-Governance-Structure]].

**Limitation:** This note was built from organizational and IA landing summaries plus the charter **URL**. The detailed duties, membership rules, meeting cadence, and explicit charter obligations were **not** transcribed here. For authoritative committee terms, read the published charter directly.

## Position in the public governance structure

Committee of [[Board of Management]] → supports board oversight distinct from [[Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer]] operational management and distinct from tax law administration (which the Board does not perform).

## Related CRA priorities

- Priority **A** (integrity) and **B** (efficiency) benefit from IA/PE assurance described at the function level ([[CRA Strategic Priorities]])

## Related published audits or evaluations

- [[Internal Audit and Program Evaluation]] — audits conducted per **International Standards for the Professional Practice of Internal Auditing** (IA landing page)

## Related business processes

- Risk-based internal audit focusing on risk management, management control framework, and information for decision-making and reporting (IA landing page)

## Related systems or data concepts

Not specified in the high-level sources used for this note.

## Source date / as_of

Charter URL verified **2026-07-23**; IA landing page modified **2026-01-23** per source summary.

## Known limitations of the public description

- **Charter content not reproduced** in this note—only the existence of a public charter and general board/IA/PE relationships from other official summaries.
- Do not infer committee powers beyond the charter and Board page without reading those documents.

# Board of Management

## Stable role information

The Board of Management is the statutory governance body publicly described as overseeing the **organization and administration** of the Canada Revenue Agency.

Official CRA material states the Board:

- Supports world-class tax and benefit administration
- Develops/approves the Corporate Business Plan; approves the Departmental Results Report and annual audited financial statements
- Oversees organization and management of the CRA
- Has **no authority** in the administration or enforcement of program/tax legislation
- May not direct the Commissioner or an employee in statutory powers
- Is not authorized to receive personal/business information obtained under program legislation

Supported by the [[Corporate Secretariat]] / Board Secretariat. See [[CRA-Governance-Structure]].

## Composition (public description)

**Fifteen directors:**

| Seat | Count |
|------|-------|
| Chair | 1 |
| Federal representatives | 2 |
| Provincial representatives | 10 |
| Territorial representative | 1 |
| Commissioner (ex officio) | 1 |

The Board **oversees organization and administration**; the **Commissioner** is accountable to the Board for **daily management** ([[Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer]]).

## Position in the public governance structure

```
Parliament ← Minister of National Revenue (accountable for CRA)
Board of Management → organization, admin, Corporate Business Plan
Commissioner and CEO → day-to-day admin & enforcement (Minister's delegated authority)
```

Tax enforcement authority rests with the Commissioner under the Minister—not with the Board.

## Related CRA priorities

Corporate Business Plan alignment with [[CRA Strategic Priorities]] and [[CRA Departmental Results Framework]].

## Related published audits or evaluations

Board oversight context for internal audit and program evaluation planning/reporting ([[Audit Committee]], [[Audit, Evaluation, and Risk Branch|AERB]]). Governance onboarding: [[CRA-Governance-Structure]] · [[Corporate Secretariat]].

## Related business processes

Corporate planning and performance reporting at agency level ([[CRA Performance Measurement]]).

## Related systems or data concepts

Board explicitly lacks access to confidential client information for enforcement (operational framework page).

## Current office holder

- **Chair / directors:** verify on the current [Board of Management](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/corporate/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/board-management.html) / biographies pages before relying on any individual name.
- **Commissioner (ex officio):** see [[Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer]] current office holder (Heather Evans as of Commissioners page 2026-07-23).

## Historical office holders

- **2025 organizational chart snapshot:** Suzanne Gouin named as Chair; Bob Hamilton named as Commissioner ex officio on that chart. Treat chart names as historical unless confirmed on a current Board/Commissioners page.
- Organization page text (2025) states Gouin’s second term ends **2026-08-28** — useful historical appointment detail, not a substitute for current confirmation after that date.

## Source dates

- **Role/structure source date:** Organization page details **2025-09-09**; Board page as linked
- **as_of_date / last_verified:** **2026-07-25**

## Known limitations of the public description

- Committee-level duties beyond high-level IA/PE oversight are limited in sources used for [[Audit Committee]].
- Do not infer reporting lines from Board–branch collaboration language in audits.

## Sources

- [Board of Management](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/corporate/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/board-management.html)
- [Organization — Ministerial transition 2025](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/corporate/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/ministerial-transition-2025/organization.html)
- [Canada Revenue Agency structure and operational framework](https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/corporate/about-canada-revenue-agency-cra/canada-revenue-agency-structure-operational-framework.html)

# Taxpayers Ombudsperson

## Stable role information

Official CRA Organization page (Agency Governance Overview / Taxpayers’ Ombudsperson sections) describes the role as:

- Operating at **arm’s length** from the CRA
- **Accountable directly to the Minister** ([[Minister of National Revenue]])
- Having **no authority** in the administration or enforcement of legislation for which the CRA remains fully accountable to the Minister
- Mandated to improve service via complaint mechanisms, systemic reporting, and outreach
- Upholding the eight service-related rights in the Taxpayer Bill of Rights

**Official organizational relationship:** Ombudsperson Liaison Office (OLO) is located in [[Service, Innovation, and Integration Branch|SIIB]]; the SIIB Assistant Commissioner, as Chief Service Officer, holds monthly bilateral meetings with the Ombudsperson.

## Position in the public governance structure

Separate from [[Board of Management]] (organization/admin oversight) and from [[Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer]] day-to-day operations. See [[CRA-Governance-Structure]].

## Current office holder

**François Boileau**, Taxpayers’ Ombudsperson — confirmed on the [Office of the Taxpayers’ Ombudsperson](https://www.canada.ca/en/taxpayers-ombudsperson.html) and in 2026 OTO news releases still naming Boileau (accessed **2026-07-25**). Term extension announced **2025-09-16**.

## Historical office holders

- Named on the **2025** ministerial transition organizational chart: François Boileau (historical snapshot; later confirmed still current by OTO pages).

## Related CRA priorities

Service fairness and trust themes align with [[CRA Vision Mission and Values]] at a thematic level.

## Related business processes

- [[Tax Administration]] and taxpayer service (high-level thematic link only)

## Source dates

- **Role/mandate source date:** Organization page details **2025-09-09**
- **Current-incumbent confirming sources:** OTO site / 2026 news releases — accessed **2026-07-25**
- **as_of_date / last_verified:** **2026-07-25**

## Known limitations of the public description

- This note does not reproduce the full complaint process or all systemic reports.
- Re-verify incumbency after future appointments.
